item.title: Another rates MD left Barclays in London after resigning earlier this week
item.description:
Barclays' London macro team has lost another managing director (MD). James Hackett, who had been there for his entire career since 2007, is understood to have resigned earlier this week. He was an MD on the rates sales desk.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Barclays declined to comment on Hackett's disappearance. Hackett didn't respond to a request to comment.
Barclays' London macro desk has a history of hedge fund exits. </news/barclays-macro-to-hedge-funds>It's not clear whether this is Hackett's intention too. His departure follows various promotions </news/barclays-performed-promotions-to-stop-macro-salespeople-joining-their-friend> on the macro sales desk last September. These included the promotion of Ben Mabley to head of rates and solutions sales, the promotion of Rumit Sawjani to co-head of hedge fund and systematic sales with Gwen Jing and the promotion of Punitha Rajah to head of UK real money sales. Rajah was only a director at the time but is thought to be one of the biggest earners on the desk.
If Hackett doesn't want to join a hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, he could try Nomura. Filippo Zorzoli, </news/nomura-s-macro-salespeople-are-apprehensive-about-their-new-boss> Barclays' former head of rates and solutions sales, is now at the Japanese bank and had been expected to hire. However, Nomura said <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-16/nomura-signals-trading-revenue-growth-is-slowing-as-boom-cools>earlier this month that it's been having a "challenging" time in rates trading.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Leaving banking for private equity is no longer aligned to the reality of the world. Continued excitement over Morgan Stanley email leak
item.description:
If you're working in banking and you're thinking of leaving for private equity </news/2019/04/move-from-banking-to-private-equity>, you should maybe think again. Private equity is not what it was. Long live careers in investment banking. </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This has been apparent for a while </news/2022/09/hedge-fund-vs-private-equity-jobs>, but Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-09-24/private-equity-jobs-lose-appeal-as-carried-interest-payouts-shrink>suggests a tipping point may have been reached now that private equity carried interest </news/what-is-carried-interest> payments are withered and dried. If you stay in banking you might get paid more in salaries and bonuses </news/investment-banking-vs-private-equity-pay-high-performers>than you will earn in private equity once carried interest is removed from the wallet. Maybe you will also work less.
This reality is slowly percolating through junior bankers, who until recently were so keen to work in private equity that they would apply for jobs in the industry before they'd even begun working in banking after leaving university/college, and would then interview through the night. </news/2022/03/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity>
Now, junior bankers are detecting that the world has changed. “These people have modelled their financial futures on a reality that isn’t materializing now,” Sloan Klein, a careers coach who works with analysts and associates </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>, told Bloomberg. “And that’s really stressful.”
It's not just juniors. In a Substack post <https://www.thecuriousmind.org/p/the-event-horizon>earlier this week, Ahmed Husain, a former Goldman Sachs' managing director who's spent the past 12 years in family offices, said that too many people working on Wall Street have made "a straight line bet on nothing changing."
Banking is full of people who are members of a "single income family with $1mm pre-tax income with a $500k burn rate," said Husain. They are "masters of the universe". They are also living paycheck to paycheck.
When the future is not like the past, Husain said this becomes particularly problematic. "The 30-year mortgage, the career built on a credential, the bond portfolio, the pension. It all works fine when the world changes 3% a year."
With the world changing faster than this, modelling your financial future on a glide path to receiving tax-efficient carried interest payments of $10m+ a year </news/private-equity-credit-pay>is no longer appropriate. You may be better off hanging around in banking, or even leaving to work with trucks.
Bloomberg spoke to one former private equity professional who now runs a company fitting equipment to trucks. Garrett Werner ran the gauntlet of working for Evercore, jumping to private equity, becoming a principal and then leaving for his truck company in Oklahoma. Werner is now aged 32 and wearing steel toe-capped boots.
This may not be for everyone. And private equity might still come through. Bloomberg notes that private equity firms are sitting on investments that are in the black but that still haven't been sold, and that if they were this would generate $17bn in carried interest payments. Working in private equity now is a bet on this happening, or on future investments being easier to exit profitably than those of the low rate world past. If this isn't for you, you can always earn a steady $251k as an associate in banking. </news/investment-banking-vs-private-equity-pay-high-performers>
Separately, Mohamed Atmani </news/mohamed-atmani-morgan-stanley> at Morgan Stanley had been having a fine year </news/morgan-stanley-md-email> until he accidentally emailed a list of potential deals with 'sensitive' prices to clients and then attempted to retract it.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/morgan-stanley-rushes-to-contain-fallout-after-deal-list-leak?srnd=homepage-americas>says that Atmani's list has come to the attention of competitors, some of whom said they will be using it to target potential clients. Regulators in China and India have reportedly starting looking at the matter. The list mostly focused on Asia and EMEA and reportedly included stalled projects and names of funds backing the deals.
Citing "people familiar with the matter" Bloomberg says Morgan Stanley itself has been holding urgent and apologetic meetings with private equity firms to assure them that the fallout will be mitigated. Maybe Atmani might want to work with flat bed trucks in Oklahoma instead.
Meanwhile...
The private equity sector is managing a record $4.7tn in assets. But a growing portion of these assets are unsold companies, the median holding time for which is now seven years. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/2b307c1e-cd98-4666-91d5-000b1dc7bbd1?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Taula Capital </news/diego-megia-taula-capital> is down 9.4% for the year through to September 18. This reverses a recovery it had made since March. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/hedge-fund-taula-down-9-4-in-volatile-year-for-macro-traders?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260924&utm_campaign=author_19458291>)
Goldman has earned more than $200m in fees this year from lending to Situational Awareness. This is more than it's earned from any other client in its prime brokerage business. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/bdec4129-ccac-4149-aa53-90ddd50cb925?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Ken Griffin wants a helicopter landing pad near his new house in Miami but people are not keen. “You are giving one person a permit for something that could be potentially annoying for a thousand.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/ken-griffin-s-miami-beach-helipad-plan-faces-resident-pushback?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5MDI1ODQ5OSwiZXhwIjoxNzkwODYzMjk5LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUTElXWUZLSzNOWUQwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiI1NjMyNTdERDBGRDQ0OUE5ODMwMDQyRDQ2Qjg0MjQzOCJ9.qNUynNmzP3jlDKXwQu8bBb_TnKEPRpN3py2pwskY26k&utm_source=whatsapp&utm_medium=social&utm_content=business&utm_campaign=giftlink>
The CFA 1 pass rate is now above 40%, which is above the average for the past 10 years. It's all about a "consistent study plan" apparently. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/cfa-first-level-pass-rate-rises-to-43-above-decade-average?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260924&utm_campaign=author_19908303>
HSBC was also providing its Hong Kong bankers with a $26k subsidy for joining private members clubs. Not any more. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/37e6c9d9-2237-468d-b0c5-18b5d09c2ccc?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
HSBC was going to have a board meeting in Dubai. It's moved it to London for safety reasons and is only allowing “business-critical” travel to the UAE. “Local executives are dealing with a lot still," said one insider. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/8b470f65-6fc3-44b6-9295-e07008ce302d?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Chandler Bocklage, head of business development at Point72, says Steve Cohen is an exceptionally inquisitive person and that working in hedge funds is a hard job. "The dedication and sacrifice is complete." (PitchThePM) <https://pitchthepm.substack.com/p/why-point72-wins-20-years-next-to?utm_source=substack&publication_id=7758668&post_id=217182070&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>

item.title: Hedge fund Jain Global paid £611k per head in London last year as profits doubled
item.description:
Hedge fund Jain Global </news/jain-global-hedge-fund-costs> has released some UK accounts and in many ways they seem pretty fine.
The fund, run by Bobby Jain </news/jain-global>, who is returning to the lap of Izzy Englander, made £9.2m in profits at Jain Global (UK) Partners last year. This was an increase in the £6m in profits Jain Global made in the previous accounting period, which ran for 16 months between the entity's formation in September 2023 and the end of December 2024.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As Jain grew, it embarked upon a hiring spree. Headcount tripled to 89 people in London. These people were paid an average of £611k each in 2025, down from the circa £900k Jain paid on an annualised basis on the previous period.
Jain Global also had five London partners, one of whom - Paul Jefferys </news/jain-global> - resigned in September last year. Another was Jain Global UK Limited, the holding company owning the LLP. The other three, who are still in place, are Ashwin Kumar, James O'Callaghan and Surendran Pathmanathan.
Jain Global's UK partners shared £9.2m in profits for 2025. However, most of this, £7.5m, appears to have gone to Jain Global (UK) Ltd, leaving the individual partners with around £2.4m between them.
The reason for Jain Global's diminshing UK average pay in the face of rising UK average profit is not clear. It's possible that the fund hired all its most expensive people first and then supplemented them with less costly recruits thereafter. The accounts say Jain likes to keep its costs flexible.
Jain Global didn't immediately respond to a request to comment.
Jain Global is now managing money only for Millennium. Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jain-global-august-performance-returns-outside-money-millennium-2026-9> reported earlier this month that it ended its life as an independent fund with a loss of 0.2%, putting 2026 returns at 3.7% until that point.

item.title: Morgan Stanley's accidental email MD had been having a great year
item.description:
It has not been a good week for Mohamed Atmani </news/mohamed-atmani-morgan-stanley> at Morgan Stanley. This is a shame, because it had been a good year.
Atmani is the managing director (MD) at Morgan Stanley in Hong Kong who sometime earlier this week accidentally sent an internal list of 100 investment banking deals that Morgan Stanley is pitching on in Asia, plus price-sensitive information, to some clients.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We have not spoken to Atmani. He is Morgan Stanley's head of financial sponsors for the Asia Pacific region, and Bloomberg said he had been intending to send out a client-facing version of the file. This version was more generic and included general updates and a list of recent transactions. Seemingly it did not include price-sensitive information.
Bloomberg said Atmani attempted to retract the message. Charlie Bouckaert, JPMorgan's global head of M&A, helpfully told Bloomberg it makes sense to "run to the fire" in these situations and to take ownership of the mistake.
It's not clear whether Atmani has spent today running to the flames, but it's worth noting both that it's an unfortunate year for this to have happened to him, and that JPMorgan is Morgan Stanley's major competitor in the Asian financial sponsors space.
Figures from data provider Dealogic show Morgan Stanley ranks first for year-to-date Asia ex-Japan financial sponsor banking revenues, which is the business that Atmani runs. This is its best ranking year-to-date since 2023. Usually, JPMorgan comes out on top. Bouckaert's comments may have contained an element of Schadenfreude.
Morgan Stanley may tolerate Atmani's error in the circumstances. It could have been worse. He could have been junior. One former banker has been recalling an incident in which an analyst accidentally sent an email accusing a fellow analyst of being a "little sh*t" to the whole firm. The best part of that incident was the follow-up emails. "Dozens of people replying to all, saying please do not reply to all. It was great on a big trading floor because people would chuckle every time one hit everyone’s inbox," the banker recalls.
Sometimes awkward emails are sent intentionally. In 2015, Justin Kwan, a second year analyst at Barclays in New York emailed incoming interns </news/2015/06/morning-coffee-2nd-year-analyst-at-barclays-sends-inappropriate-email-to-interns-big-banking-job-growth-in-london> suggesting that they might find themselves sleeping beneath desks. The email went viral but doesn't appear to have damaged Kwan's career; he now works for a major private equity firm in New York.

item.title: Susquehanna hired another C++ legend after Bjarne Stroustrup
item.description:
Where can you find the most exciting C++ jobs? </news/low-latency-c>Recent hires at Susquehanna are helping the electronic trading firm </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>make a strong case for itself. Last month, it hired Bjarne Stroustrup, </news/a-high-frequency-trading-firm-just-hired-bjarne-stroustrup-creator-of-c> the language's creator. Now it has hired a long-serving principal engineer at Microsoft who is also well respected in the C++ community.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Gabriel Dos Reis joined Susquehanna as a technical fellow, the same role held by Stroustrup. Susquehanna says he "will collaborate with teams across the organization on modern C++ practices, architecture and the continued evolution of the systems that support Susquehanna’s business."
At Microsoft, Dos Reis was an architect for Visual Studio, Microsoft's integrated development environment. He's also a PhD mathematician from the Grande Écoles, </news/2023/02/best-grande-ecole-finance>having studied at Ecole Normale Supérieure.
Dos Reis has spent just shy of three decades on the C++ standards committee and made some significant contributions to the language. Herb Sutter, a technical fellow at Citadel Securities and former head of the standards committee, said his work with Stroustrup on the constexpr function </news/citadel-securities-c-26#:~:text=C%2B%2B%20has%20been%20updated%20seven%20times%20since%201998%3B%20C%2B%2B%2026%20will%20be%20the%20eighth.%20Sutter%20says%20C%2B%2B%2026%20is%20the%20language%27s%20most%20important%20iteration%20since%20C%2B%2B%2011%2C%20when%20Bjarne%20Stroustrup%20and%20Gabriel%20Dos%20Reis%C2%A0introduced%20the%20contexpr%20function.%C2%A0>is the most significant change to C++ of the past 15 years.
When announcing his arrival at Susquehanna, Stroustrup said that financial services "places extraordinary demands on performance, reliability, and maintainability, making it one of the most interesting applications of modern software engineering." Susquehanna says C++ powers "many of the systems and tools used across trading, research and risk management."

item.title: Jane Street CTO: "Everyone knows some Python... lots of people aren't any good at it."
item.description:
Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>'s continual evolution is not only happening on the trading floor </news/2023/11/sam-bankman-fried-jane-street-culture>. The market making firm has made significant changes to its engineering culture in recent years by introducing Python, </news/python-ocaml-jane-street-ai> which has been very useful for the firm's machine learning efforts, but presents a few other problems.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"One of the things I worry about is people getting captured by their tools," said Jane Street CTO Ron Minsky on the firm's podcast, Signals and Threads <https://signalsandthreads.com/learning-goals-and-the-goals-of-learning-teaching-in-the-age-of-ai/>, this week. Jane Street has used functional language OCaml </news/2023/11/ocaml-vs-c-high-frequency-trading>for decades and made sure that everyone knew the language so that they "can go anywhere into any code base and do stuff." Thanks to Python, Minsky said there has been a "natural striation where people get good at the one thing," but aren't necessarily plug-and-play. Minsky said "I'd really love to be more in a world where there are no OCaml programmers and Python programmers... just software engineers."
Unlike OCaml, Python is not a niche language. In fact, it's the most popular language there is, </news/programming-languages-jobs-banks-finance> topping the TIOBE index. <https://www.tiobe.com/tiobe-index/> "Everyone knows Python," Minsky said, "but there are lots of people who aren't any good at it and there's real things to learn to be good at it." He said there are also "people who've been [at Jane Street] for a long time," who may not have had the need to learn Python until very recently.
Aaron Bauer, a developer educator at Jane Street, said on the podcast that a lot of the work researchers and traders do in Python is via notebooks: "there are different notebook solutions [but] they all have different significant flaws or limitations." One common limitation is that the code in these notebooks is "not always easily shareable," but Bauer said Jane Street is building a solution to fix this.
It's not just the languages changing at Jane Street, it's the nature of the coding process. </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing>Minsky said that "the modern condition of a software engineer" involves "a lot more [code] review as a proportion of your time" thanks to agentic coding tools. Minsky said it's a "real problem" when engineers "vibe it up too much and use LLMs to generate stuff and do not think." He said that AI generated programs can be "uncanny" in that it can look well written and presentable, have very few inidications that there would be a problem with the code and yet "they're often still super broken."

item.title: Stripe has put an ex-HSBC compliance guy in charge of its UK business
item.description:
Compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance>people in banks today are some of the people most at-risk of being displaced by AI. </news/ai-in-compliance-finance> Some compliance people who left for fintech </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech> appear to be having a much better time.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Marc Fungard announced that he has become CEO of the UK entity of payments giant Stripe. </news/stripe-high-performance-engineers> He has spent the last three and a half years at Stripe in London and concurrently holds the role of global head of financial crime, compliance and risk oversight. Before that, he spent eight years at HSBC, where he was global head of its financial intelligence unit, then its global head of compliance analytics. Fungard also spent over a decade working for the US government in a variety of roles; he spent four years as director of the office for illicit finance within the US Treasury.
He replaces Stephen O'Callaghan, based in Stripe's Dublin headquarters, who had been CEO of the UK arm for over two years. He announced via LinkedIn that he has become CEO of Stripe's European arm, 'Stripe Technology Europe Ltd.' For now, O'Callaghan is still registered as a director on the UK entity whereas Fungard is not. The firm did not respond to a request for comment.
O'Callaghan doesn't come from a bank like Fungard, but he does have a background in accounting; he started his career at Big Four firm EY, then worked across the finance teams of Google and Meta before becoming Stripe's head of international accounting from 2015 to 2020.
They're both intriguing picks to run the UK business, which is largely populated with technologists and salespeople. Its most recent accounts on Companies House, for 2024, </news/stripe-s-average-uk-pay-260k-including-92k-in-stock> showed that it had 288 employees of which 204 worked in sales or tech. Stripe's accounts don't make any disclosures around executive pay, but the average total compensation for employees in the UK entity was £260k that year.

item.title: Forgotten London hedge fund appears to be progressively shrinking
item.description:
A century ago, Hilaire Belloc wrote <https://www.gutenberg.org/files/65304/65304-h/65304-h.htm> about how Roman infrastructure disappeared from Britain; not with an explosion, but with a gradual erosion reflecting neither the will nor knowledge to repair it. The modern hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> industry is far removed from those times, but principles, seemingly, are timeless.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
TT International Asset Management Ltd, the hedge fund group founded by former Fidelity investment director Tim Tacchi, published its 2025 results earlier this week. They didn't seem good: revenue declined by 7% to £32m ($43m), the fourth straight year of decline and less than its 2021 high of £79m ($104m).
The results said that profit also continued to fall, and the firm recorded a £10m ($13m) loss for 2025, up from the £9m ($11m) loss recorded in 2024. In 2021, it recorded a £22m ($30m) profit. Headcount also decreased by 7%, after four years of growth, to 101 people.
The only part of the business seemingly not in decline according to the results is its pay per head, which nudged upwards slightly, from £249k ($329k) to £250k ($331k). Adjusted for inflation, however, that was also in its fourth straight year of decline.
The diminution of everything was related to a fall in assets under management (AuM). TT International said that it ended the year with around $5bn, below its $7bn group-level breakeven value, after a “challenging year for asset gathering”. It’s worth noting that the hedge fund industry as a whole reached an all-time high for AUM in 2025 of around $5tn, according to Hedge Fund Research <https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/hedge-funds-now-manage-record-almost-5-trillion-says-hfr-2025-10-23/>. “2025 was challenging for all active asset management firms,” TT International said in its filing.
Scenarios for 2026 are unclear. “Under adverse scenarios, the Group maintains surplus capital and meets regulatory requirements,” TT International said, and there “are also available management actions that can be enacted if necessary.” TT International did not respond to a request for comment.
TT International’s owner, which since 2019 has been Japanese bank SMBC, might have a raised eyebrow. It bought a hedge fund with $8.4bn in AuM back then. Since then, aside from AuM, the fund has also lost its longtime CEO, Eric Mackay, to self-employment. At least it still has Tim Tacchi </news/2013/01/downton-abbey-envy-alive-and-well-at-banker-country-homes>.

item.title: Morgan Stanley's Singapore macro desk lost up to 40 people. Now it has new bosses
item.description:
As we reported here not long ago, Morgan Stanley's macro team has lost at least 40 people </news/morgan-stanley-s-macro-team-actually-lost-far-more-people-than-we-thought>, many of them in Singapore. Now it's had a shakeup.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/morgan-stanley-reshuffle-leadership-of-asia-macro-trading-desk?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260924&utm_campaign=author_16830521> reports that Morgan Stanley has reshuffled the leadership of its macro desk. Rahul Gautam, who - we understand and as per his LinkedIn profile - was previously head of fixed income and equities trading in South East Asia, will now simply be head of Morgan Stanley's international commodities trading business and co-head of South East Asian equities.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This looks like a narrower role for Gautam. It's not clear whether he welcomes it. Bloomberg says the bulk of Morgan Stanley's fixed income trading activities in Asia - comprising FX and emerging markets rates trading - have now been transplanted to Sherry Xu and Roland Jeurissen. Xu and Jeurissen are two existing Morgan Stanley traders and they are now effectively handling most of Morgan Stanley's fixed income business in the region.
The changes are thought to have been overseen by Samer Oweida, Morgan Stanley's New York based head of FX and emerging markets, to whom Bloomberg says Xu and Jeurissen will now report.
They will also report to Niall Almeida, Morgan Stanley's Asia head of fixed income, currencies and commodities (FICC), who also covers the smaller credit business.
Gautam, meanwhile, will return to focus on his earlier domain of equities trading, with commodities appended to it.
There are many opportunities in Asian markets </news/singapore-macro-hiring> this year and hedge funds are hiring. Many of Morgan Stanley's circa 40 leavers have since arrived elsewhere. Bloomberg notes that Sahil Aggarwal </news/morgan-stanley-s-singapore-trading-team-lost-a-lot-of-people>, Morgan Stanley's former Asia head of linear rates trading, who left in June, has, for example, now joined hedge fund Verition. Aggarwal was only promoted to managing director at Morgan Stanley in January.
Morgan Stanley didn't respond to a request to comment.

item.title: "The analysts at my investment bank would rather be cut than promoted to associate"
item.description:
I work at a European investment bank </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>. For analysts </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> here, being let go has become a more attractive outcome than being promoted to associate. I can't speak for everyone's intentions, but people seem way more enthusiastic about finding a way out </news/finance/overwork-banking> than finding a way up.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It's not just about finding a big new role in somewhere like private equity. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> This still features in the conversation, but some talk about leaving without the next prestigious role lined up. One new joiner tried to resign after just three days. That's a short period in which to assess a career in banking, but might be long enough to form an opinion about a team.
It's not hard to see why people want to leave: the workload is substantial. There's always a great deal to do, which provides plenty of experience and learning opportunities. However, the time available for someone more senior to actually check your analysis is much less substantial. Juniors are expected to just get on with it, which doesn't give them much reassurance that they're actually learning anything. Although it's an environment where you can learn a lot, it's not one that a lot of people want to continue learning in.
If the bank sees people leave its program and take up flashy jobs elsewhere, it might think that the training is actually working. For the analysts themselves, the desire to leave is much more significant than the desire to work somewhere new.
Jean-Luc Jones is a pseudonym

item.title: Morning Coffee: Morgan Stanley MD’s accidental terrible mistake. Being a hedge fund analyst is no longer such a terrible job
item.description:
Everyone who works in an email job has a recurring stress nightmare of pressing “reply to all” or otherwise sending a message to someone who it really wasn’t intended for. Bankers are no exception, so the collective intake of breath yesterday on behalf of Mohamed Atmani, Morgan Stanley’s APAC head of financial sponsors <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-23/morgan-stanley-investment-bank-deal-list-leaked-in-email-misfire> could be heard all around the financial world.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It seems that Atmani sent out a “deals list” to some clients, identifying some potential IPOs and other deals which Morgan Stanley was pitching for or monitoring, across the Asian and EMEA markets. This isn’t necessarily a big deal <https://x.com/valueterminal/status/2102776367054008702?s=20> in itself – any firm that’s considering an IPO already knows that they are, and knows that Morgan Stanley knows. In many ways, the whole purpose of maintaining a deals list is to be able to talk knowledgably to clients about what’s going on in the market. Intrinsically, this is the sort of “confidential information” which most people wouldn’t read if you sent it to them Federal Express, and which anyone who cares about it could always piece together from news reports and industry gossip.
What caused the problem is that Atmani apparently sent out the internal version of the deals list, which may have contained what Bloomberg calls “extensive price-sensitive information” on some of these deals. Morgan Stanley is certainly taking it seriously, saying that “we promptly took steps to address this inadvertent sharing of information and we continue to engage with relevant parties”.
It’s not clear what the troublesome information might have been. Deal pipeline lists don’t usually go into much detail on financials and M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> bankers tend to keep quiet about bids which haven’t been announced yet even internally. But they might include updates on valuation and investor interest, and some of these might be a bit embarrassing if they include things which weren’t intended for wider distribution.
The real problem is the embarrassment. On the sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> side of things, this kind of mistake is called a “fat finger”, and they are sometimes quickly forgiven and forgotten because everyone understands that in a fast moving high-pressure environment, mistakes are inevitable. But investment bankers tend to pride themselves on their care and attention to detail; their fingers are meant to be elegant and slim. In a world in which fully grown adults have been known to lose their temper over precise shades of yellow in highlighted spreadsheet rows, a mistake like this is an unpleasant reminder of human imperfection.
Atmani has been around long enough not to have his career entirely defined by something like this – he’s been an MD since 2010 and worked at UBS and Deutsche </news/2017/04/deutsche-bank-hired-an-md-from-ubs> before moving to Morgan Stanley. There will be some humble pie to be eaten, and some financial sponsors may decide to put business somewhere else for a quarter. But everyone makes mistakes. And the one thing we know about email mistakes is that they are governed by a particularly strict version of the law of karma; if you laugh at someone else for making one, you are pretty much bound to do the same thing yourself sooner rather than later.
Elsewhere, it’s occasionally been said that hedge fund analysts share a motto with the Hells Angels – “when we do right nobody remembers, when we do wrong nobody forgets”. Portfolio managers are the ones who pick and choose which of an analyst’s ideas to back. This means that they are well placed to take the credit for the good ideas while dodging the blame for the bad. And even if your PM allows an “I told you so” when the idea they passed on turns out to be a massive success, they still haven’t got any profits to pay your bonus out of. It’s an extremely frustrating job </news/analyst-hedge-fund>.
That might be about to change though. Ryan Walsh <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hedge-fund-talent-war-set-to-push-analyst-pay-above-10m-74405804?mod=topic_news>, a former Millennium PM now runs a talent agency called Laurel Lake Advisors. Walsh thinks that “top analysts have just as much leverage as portfolio managers”, while his colleague Ben Sharples is predicting a “talent war for analysts” in the future. The two say that analysts can be underpaid in job moves by “multiples of what would originally be underwritten” and even forecast that we will see $10m packages for hedge fund analysts in the near future. People will put up with a lot of frustration for that kind of money.
Meanwhile …
Raja Akram of Deutsche Bank says “I don’t quite get the gloomy outlook”. He confirms (along with several others on the Street) that Q3 will be a bit more muted than the first half of the year, but suggests that it’s in line with internal expectations and budget. Perhaps analyst estimates just got a bit carried away with themselves. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/deutsche-cfo-akram-says-investment-bank-will-be-flat-in-q3-but-outlook-isnt-gloomy-5bc64726?mod=topic_news>)
Confessions of an accidental bonus basher – how did the economic case for the EU bonus cap and other similar regulations actually get made? (FT Alphaville <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/deutsche-cfo-akram-says-investment-bank-will-be-flat-in-q3-but-outlook-isnt-gloomy-5bc64726?mod=topic_news>)
The saying is always that strategy is an opinion but real estate is a fact, and Qube Research & Trading is the latest quant fund to put money where its mouth is and commit to a lot of expensive office space. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-23/qrt-expands-london-office-as-hedge-funds-compete-for-prime-space?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260923&utm_campaign=author_22490032>)
Could UBS really leave Switzerland? It might be argued that after the recent capital requirements changes, it can’t afford not to. (Breakingviews <https://www.breakingviews.com/columns/breaking-view/ubs-capital-loss-puts-radical-options-table-2026-09-23/>)
Perhaps not the hero we deserve, but Jay Jones is the hero we need. Under the alias of “The Profiler”, he’s made it his mission to spot recruitment scams. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/tech/the-vigilante-whos-taking-down-recruitment-scammers-one-fake-job-ad-at-a-time-e441b100?mod=mhp>)
Charlie Bouckaert, JP Morgan’s global head of M&A, says the question isn’t whether the 2026 deals boom will continue but rather “what’s going to throw us off now”? Which gives us our earworm for the day <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i2FW1WJc0lg>. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-23/jpmorgan-global-m-a-head-bouckaert-sees-tremendous-levels-of-deals-continuing>)

item.title: Deutsche Bank's fixed income traders also have excuses, amidst cost cutting
item.description:
Deutsche Bank's shares are down nearly 1% today. The decline is attributable to a speech given this morning at the Bank of America financials conference by CFO Raja Akram. In it, Akram said September has been a "mixed bag" in fixed income trading and that revenues across Deutsche's investment bank are likely to be "flattish or slightly down" on last year.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
People with keen memories will recall that Brian Moynihan, the fun-loving CEO </news/brian-moynihan-bank-of-america>of Bank of America, said something similar </news/bank-of-america-q3> at the Barclays conference a few weeks ago. Fixed income sales and trading revenues were down and erratic, said Brian. BofA's share price fell 6% at one point after that.
It's an unfortunate time of year for things to lose their vigour, what with bonus decisions being made in the next few months. As we observed earlier this week, though, Bank of America's fixed income traders have some good excuses </news/bank-of-america-fixed-income-poor-performance> for their poor performance. These are centered around the fact that the bank as a whole hasn't done much in the way of lending to the ever-expanding AI ecosystem, and that they therefore haven't enjoyed the trading volumes that result from being allied too major issuers in the sector.
Akram's speech today suggests that Deutsche Bank's traders may also have excuses. Like BofA's fixed income traders, they are stronger in credit trading. Unlike BofA's traders, they don't seem to be using the AI underwriting card. Instead, Akram pointed to the fact that Q3 2025 was a record quarter for them, and that even if Q3 2026 is only similarly good, it will still be great.
This is a good excuse. As the chart below shows, Deutsche Bank's fixed income sales and trading revenues were indeed at a record high last year. However, they also appear due for a fall.
The softening in the fixed income bicep comes as Akram said today that new opportunities for cutting costs are appearing. At Deutsche Bank's Investor Deep Dive (known by the acronym IDD) last year, </news/deutsche-bank-s-investor-day> the bank said it expected to increase costs by 2% by 2028.
Speaking today, Akram explained that new cost-cutting opportunities which were "not fully appreciated" previously are now in play.
These involve AI. AI can particularly be used for "transaction monitoring and the credit underwriting process," said Akram. And when it's used, entire systems can be redesigned. These include people, "where those people are sitting, high-cost location, low-cost location, what they're doing."
In the circumstances, it sounds helpful to have an excuse for only moderately good performance, even if your area doesn't obviously lend itself to reimagining.
Akram also said today that Deutsche Bank doesn't let everyone there have access to the best AI models. Only engineers and software engineers get to the use the advanced models, he said. "The majority of our general population has access to tools that are sufficient for their need."

item.title: Scotiabank hired a tough new sales head in New York
item.description:
If you want to hire yourself a brand new sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> managing director (MD), you’ll want to hire a big shot. A hard hitter. A heavyweight, even. Sometimes you get one, and sometimes they can also knock most people’s lights out.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Toussaint Davis joined Scotiabank last week as an MD and head of its emerging markets international sales team. He joined the Canadian bank from Morgan Stanley in New York, where he was also an emerging markets sales MD. Neither Davis nor Scotiabank responded to a request for comment.
Davis has some interesting hobbies. He raised <https://haymakersforhope.org/events/boxing/nyc-2019/fighters/toussaint-davis-9tnh9n> over $20k for “Haymakers for Hope”, a charity that organises boxing matches between amateurs to raise money for charity. His profile on the Haymakers for Hope website lists him as 6’5” (196cm) and 220lbs (100kg), making him a particularly tough cookie – around the same size as a young Lennox Lewis.
Davis won his fight <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=voI183nvvqQ> in Haymakers for Hope by unanimous vote against Reed Edmiston, a management consultant at media and marketing consultancy Medialink back in 2019.
Davis is also a client of BULLRING <https://www.bullringcoaching.com/clients>, a performance & physical coaching company based in London that deals with “modern alpha males”, offering “power with perspective”, in its own words. “High performers often push forward relentlessly, ignoring the red flags and derailing their chances of sustainable success,” the firm’s literature says <https://www.bullringcoaching.com/about>.

item.title: The ex-Deutsche Bank saleswoman rehousing portfolio managers in Dubai
item.description:
If you're a portfolio manager thinking of leaving London for Dubai, Francesca Petrucci can assist you. Petrucci is in Dubai. She is married to a portfolio manager. And until November 2025 she was working for Deutsche Bank in London, where she spent the previous 12.5 years building a career in hedge fund rates sales </news/sales-trading-banking-ai>.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Working as a real estate agent isn't quite the same as working in hedge fund sales and Petrucci says she is still settling in to her new career. "What I miss most is saying that I work in hedge fund sales," she admits.
The trouble with working in hedge fund sales, though, is the hours. Petrucci, who has two young children, says she spent half her Deutsche Bank salary on a nanny when she was working in London. If you want to thrive in sales, she says you ideally need to go out with clients at least twice a week, </news/graham-ambrose-goldman-sachs-fitness?utm_source=chatgpt.com> preferably after work. This means leaving the house at 6.45am and returning after 10pm. "All my colleagues would be doing this, but once I had kids I wanted to see them," she says.
By comparison, as a real estate agent in Dubai, Petrucci pays lower childcare costs and has more control over her time. She says childcare in Dubai is a quarter of the price of childcare in London and she now manages her own schedule. There are viewings in the morning, before the London market opens, and contract signings in the afternoons.
It's not the same as hedge fund sales, but Petrucci is still selling to hedge fund managers. She says portfolio managers are returning to the Middle East </news/dubai-hedge-fund-manager-everyone-in-the-uae-has-an-exit-the-war-is-not-a-problem> after the panic in March </news/cost-of-getting-out-of-dubai-hedge-funds> and that the "fear has passed and everything is normal."
Much of Petrucci's work comes via word of mouth. If you too want to move to Dubai, she can help house you. Alternatively, if you're a female rates salesperson in London looking for an exit, she can show you the way.

item.title: The private credit partner that had a "dismal" job and lived with his parents as a graduate
item.description:
If you missed the boat on an internship </news/internship-investment-bank> in banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> during your undergraduate, you might be considering an MBA </news/what-s-the-point-of-an-mba-for-banking-jobs>for a shot a redemption. Many of the most successful people in finance have been in your shoes, including Michael Gatto, partner at private credit </news/private-credit> investment firm Silver Point Capital.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In a video released by Restructuring Newsletter <https://x.com/Restructuring__/status/2101360226460967089?s=20>, Gatto described his beginnings in finance. He graduated from Cornell University with no job </news/finance-job-no-internship>: "I was doing data input, it was dismal. I was living with my parents." He said he was able to "reinvent" himself by doing an MBA at Columbia, which helped get into Citi's "phenomenal credit training program." Rather than going into an active investment role after completing the program, he said that he was pushed into a role to modernize that course, which he didn't want to do.
Gatto ended up enjoying it, and doing well enough in that role to teach full time; he would go around to all of the banks assisting their education programs. Eventually, Goldman Sachs </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> offered him a job in its special situations group but, following the collapse of Long Term Capital Management, his role was eliminated before he even joined the firm. Gatto was able to find an arrangement where he worked as a contractor to keep his job at the firm, technically working as a "receptionist." When Ed Mulé, a Goldman partner and head of his group, left to co-found Silver Point Capital, Gatto came along with him.
The landscape for graduate jobs in finance today is very different but there are lessons to be learned. You can get ahead by teaching, rather than doing; analysts in banks today have complained that much of their roles have been reduced to teaching more senior people in banks about how to use AI. </news/leopold-aschenbrenner-citadel#:~:text=Elsewhere%2C%20summer%20interns,begin%20a%20career.>
However, MBAs aren't necessarily as useful as they once were. At Columbia, just 37% of 2025 MBA graduates </news/best-mba-for-finance-banking> actually went on to work in finance. The "dismal" data input job Gatto started out with has also presumably been replaced by AI. Your best bet is still to get an undergraduate internship... if you can.

item.description:
It's ok. Damien Courvalin is safe. He is not forever out of the market after a foray into a hedge fund. </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> He is at PIMCO
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥

Courvalin was last seen at Balyasny Asset Management (BAM), where he worked for three years and ran a 'Commodities Intelligence Group' before leaving unexpectedly in March. </news/goldman-sachs-to-balyasny> Courvalin's BAM departure was unexpected because he previously spent 16 years at Goldman Sachs, where he was a managing director (MD) and something of a star.

When Goldman commodities MDs contemplate moving to the buyside in the future, they can therefore choose Deighton at BAM or Courvalin at PIMCO. Or they could just join Anthony Dewell at Millennium. </news/citadel-vs-millennium>

item.title: Things are finally looking up for UK quant fund Winton
item.description:
If you’ve ever walked through Athens or Rome and felt like you were walking through the ruins of a long-forgotten and maybe superior civilization, then you might capture the same feeling walking through Kensington, the headquarters of <https://www.winton.com/news/winton-london-hq-relocates-to-knightsbridge> the hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> known as Winton.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Accounts were released earlier this week for Winton Capital Management (WCM), the main UK subsidiary for Sir David Harding’s Winton Group. The topline figures for 2025 were pretty good: revenue grew for the second year in a row, from £86m ($115m) to £101m ($135m), and operating profit increased from £10m ($13m) to £14m ($19m).
Not bad, but a far cry from Winton’s highs in the 2010’s. Back in 2014, the fund’s revenue peaked at approximately £631m (around $1bn at the time).
WCM’s headcount told a similar story. 161 souls in 2025 were up on the 157 that the firm employed in 2024, and it was the third consecutive year of headcount growth at the firm. But it was a significant decrease on its mid-2010s highs; the fund boasted 385 people in 2016, a number that halved within just five years </news/finance/winton-capital-management-profits-pay-headcount-surges>.
Was there anything to be optimistic about at Winton? Yes, there was: pay. WCM paid its people an average of £344k ($457k) across 2025, an 11% increase on the £311k ($413k) it paid on average in 2024. It was also a decline on WCM’s all-time highest average pay package, which was £428k ($569k) in 2022, but not quite as drastic a decline as revenue or headcount.
As we have touched on, Winton is far from its glory days. Winton Group Limited, the parent company owned by Sir David, paid out £5.8m ($7.7m) in dividends. Sir David is a majority, but not entire owner of Winton Group Limited; he earned £60m from the firm in 2010 and £87m from it in 2011, according to the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/ca73ff3a-e7e7-11e3-b923-00144feabdc0?syn-25a6b1a6=1>.
What happened to Winton? The firm profited in its early years from “trend-following”, a rather boring but profitable quantitative strategy that basically aimed to front-run persistent market trends – oil is steadily going up, so buy oil. Sir David switched away from the system in 2018 due to lackluster returns in preceding years, moving to a broader mix of quantitative strategies.

item.title: Citadel, the hedge fund, paid an average of $1.2m in London last year, and hired investment staff
item.description:
It's been the case for long years now that when hiring happens in financial services, it typically happens most in the middle and back office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>as organisations stock up on technologists and support staff. Citadel's various UK entities are bucking that trend.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As we reported earlier this week </news/citadel-citadel-securities-deferrals>, UK Citadel's entities have been filing their accounts with Companies House. The final set of 2025 accounts for Citadel Management (Europe) II, which is the managing corporate member that employs most of Citadel's people in London, have now been unveiled. In combination with the rest, they show Citadel's UK operations stocking up on investment professionals last year, while adding fewer support staff.
While this happened, Citadel (unsurprisingly) hiked average pay. The firm has three entities in London which disclose compensation and hea count spending: Citadel Management (Europe) II, Citadel Management (Europe) III and Citadel Enterprise Europe Services Limited.
They all do something a bit different. Citadel Enterprise Europe Services is the admin arm. Citadel Management Europe II provides services related to investment management. Citadel Management Europe III provides services and support relating to investment management, including algorithm design.
This is what pay at each body looked like last year:
If you work for Citadel in London, therefore, you want to work within Citadel Management (Europe) II (CMEL II), which employs the investment staff and pays $2m a head. But even Citadel's support entity (CEES) pays nearly $600k a head. Both are averages.
This is what Citadel pays in wages and salaries. The real money at the firm in London, however, is paid to its 24 partners. Last year, they shared $337m in profits or an average of $14m each. That's a lot, but less than in 2024 when they received an average of $21m each.
Citadel's reduced pay for London partners followed a 29% decline in group operating profit in the UK last year, which the firm said was the result of lower "performance based revenues." At the same time, operating expenses rose 32%, driven partly by paying all the new staff.
Citadel globally generated returns of 10.2% last year, versus 15.1% in 2024.

item.title: Hudson River Trading paid £820k per head to its UK staff and spent £2.4m per head on equipment
item.description:
Hudson River Trading </news/the-coffee-run-the-kind-trading-firm-paying-1m-to-graduates-and-100m-to-its-top-people> insiders told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-09-10/how-jason-carroll-built-hudson-river-trading-and-a-27-billion-fortune> earlier this month that the firm's culture is a bit like 'luxury communism' due to its egalitarian pay </news/hudson-river-trading-pay> structure. </news/how-much-do-electronic-trading-jobs-really-pay> Recent accounts for the electronic trading firm </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>'s UK entities suggest that this is a slight exaggeration.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
HRT has filed accounts for 2025 across three entities, 'Hudson River Trading Europe Ltd,' 'HRT Research Ltd' and 'HRTSVC Ltd.' Headcount across the three entities rose to 165 from 152 in 2024, but pay across the three entities was not distributed evenly.
The highest paying entity was HRT research, which "provides research and technology services." The entity paid 22 employees an average of £1.69m; it paid 24 employees an average of £944k in 2024.
HRT Europe is the firm's proprietary trading arm. It paid 21 employees an average of £1.47m. HRTSVC, which "support[s] the global trading platform used by related companies," is the largest entity by headcount and paid 122 employees an average of £550k. Across all entities, average pay was £820k.
HRT isn't just increasing spending on wages. HRTSVC's cash flow statement showed £391m of additional spending, equivalent to £2.4m per head, on 'property plant and equipment.' This might be spending on AI infrastrucutre; </news/how-ai-is-affecting-careers-in-electronic-trading-and-hft>now-expired job listings at HRT have said the firm has "very high GPU </news/programming-languages-machine-learning-ai-quant>-to-research ratios" and "triple-digit petabyte-scale storage."

item.title: Morning Coffee: Goldman Sachs’ new banking head seems a bit unusual. A sudden decline in prospects for ECM bankers
item.description:
Eyebrows might have been raised in the London investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> community yesterday, at the news that Simon Lyons <https://www.reuters.com/world/goldman-appoints-simon-lyons-uk-investment-banking-co-head-2026-09-22/> has been appointed as co-head of UK investment banking by Goldman Sachs. </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> Lyons will jointly head up the division with Nimesh Khiroya and will join the firm as a partner.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
That’s not entirely surprising. It is unusual for GS to make lateral hires at partner level, but by no means unknown. Only 50% of Goldman Sachs' last partner class </news/goldman-sachs-partners-list-2024> joined the firm as graduates. Lyons has things to recommend him. He was previously the co-head of Europe at Ardea, and had been selected as one of the founding partners when Paul Taubman set up PJT Partners in 2015. Before that he was making it rain at UBS and he’s still bringing in the big deals, most recently the acquisition of Mitie Group by OCS.
At no point until now, though, has Lyons worked for Goldman. Bringing in a head of the business from outside when you have plenty of bankers already will always ruffle feathers. And Goldman Sachs has been doing quite a lot of this recently, particularly in the EMEA region. The co-head of investment banking for France and Benelux is David Benichou, a lateral hire from Morgan Stanley and the co-head of European M&A is Carsten Woehrn, formerly of JPMorgan.
It’s not that Goldman was floundering or in any obvious need of new blood. So far in 2026, it’s captured its highest market share in EMEA deals for a decade, and it’s ranked number one in UK M&A ever before Simon Lyons starts making a contribution.
Why hire Lyons externally then? Maybe it's a declaration of intent. Maybe Goldman has identified EMEA as a region where the revenue potential is underestimated, and decided to invest enough to build a strong franchise into an utterly dominant one?
This is a strategy. It’s just not very … not very Goldman Sachs. Historically, the firm has preferred to build its talent pipeline internally, rather than to hire “galacticos” on the open market – it’s been more of a Barcelona than a Real Madrid, more of an Arsenal than a Manchester City, to use two suitably European analogies. Top level investment banking is a market made up of personal franchises and trusted relationships, but that doesn’t mean it’s always a good idea to grow that way.
Investment banking is a team sport, and however much you emphasise social skills and cultural fit in the selection process, you can never really tell how someone’s going to adapt to a new working environment until they are there. Every lateral hire of this kind takes up a partnership slot which someone else might have been hoping for. When you add that to the intrinsically destabilising effect of creating a co-head structure, the risks are considerable. Goldman has decided to take them.
Elsewhere, it does seem that there might be a few fluffy clouds <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-22/derailed-ipo-plans-rattle-us-market-ahead-of-anthropic-debut> on the previously bright horizon of the global equity capital markets industry. Market attention has mainly been focused on the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI, which were meant to be fee-earners on the scale of SpaceX in the second half. Both now appear to have both been somewhat slow in making the filings to start the process.
It's not just the fear of AI apocalypse that's issuers. Smaller deals in industries as varied as nuclear power and insurance services have also been postponed, simply because of “market conditions”. Sellers (particularly private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> backers) have a price in mind, and they seem to be worrying if they will be able to achieve it. Although the stock market itself is still doing fine, with the NASDAQ at all time highs, big investors appear worried about committing large amounts of new cash.
All of which is likely to continue while the big AI deals are overhanging the market. If OpenAI and Anthropic can sort out their “alignment” problems and move forward, then 2027 could still be a good year. If not, then the party might be about to get a little less raucous.
Meanwhile …
Not so long ago, Jefferies was the upstart on Wall Street, aggressively hiring Managing Directors from bigger firms. Now it’s getting a little of the same treatment, with Drew Weisman, Steve Tricarico, Russ Shoemaker and Hub Orr all going to Raymond James within a short space of time. (Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/raymond-james-hires-several-senior-investment-bankers-jefferies-sources-say-2026-09-21/>)
Commuting costs money, and so does childcare. The union representing Barclays workers is asking the company to recognise this, and either pay more, help out with vouchers or reduce the number of compulsory in-office days for employees with caring responsibilities or who are located a long way from their teams. (Fortune <https://fortune.com/2026/09/22/barclays-staff-demanding-more-money-return-to-office-compensation-410-weekly-cost-childcare-commuting/>)
Bankers used to moan about being unpopular, but AI employees have to deal with the mental strain of coming to terms with the fact that they might be about to destroy humanity. The news that the IPOs are delayed isn’t cheering either, apparently. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/60870960-f433-48ca-bc2c-708686a69ae7?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
“I have seen a shift in understanding on the fixed-income side about how to start pricing in climate from the physical standpoint, and that’s a big shift from five years ago to today”. Sarah Kapnick, global head of climate advisory at JPM, makes the case that it’s no longer so much a matter of ESG scores as “has the collateral been destroyed by a flood”. (Bloomberg <https://I%20have%20seen%20a%20shift%20in%20understanding%20on%20the%20fixed-income%20side%20about%20how%20to%20start%20pricing%20in%20climate%20from%20the%20physical%20standpoint,%20and%20that’s%20a%20big%20shift%20from%20five%20years%20ago%20to%20today>)
It turns out that if you make an AI clone of your boss to interact with, your actual boss is likely to hate it. And then the AI clone picks up on this hatred, and begins to hate itself. (WIRED <https://www.wired.com/story/ai-coworker-bots-loved-improv-and-interstellar-soundtrack/>)
Kids these days … more and more students are giving up on homework if it seems too long or difficult. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/b30eb538-b5a3-4fb2-bae2-785273bfda1c?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)

item.title: Goldman Sachs wants C++ specialists for a new high-frequency market making team
item.description:
Last week, </news/jpmorgan-high-frequency-trading-jobs>we noted that JPMorgan seems to be pushing into high-frequency market making. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm#:~:text=What%20are%20electronic,it%20adds%20up.> It's not alone.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Job listings at Goldman Sachs show the bank is building a "new business line" in its electronic market making group as part of a "major, multi-phase ETF initiative." It's currently hiring engineers to build the infrastructure for that business line in New York; Goldman declined to comment, but listings have a significant focus on low-latency infrastructure. Candidates need experience building "high-performance research infrastructure for very large data inputs." The bank wants C++ experts </news/low-latency-c>for this and will flat out reject you if most of your experience is in Java. Ouch.
The project seems to be focused on US ETFs; "international ETF expansion" is described as a future phase. This is enemy territory dominated by the growing algorithmic trading firms like Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>and Citadel Securities. </news/citadel-citadel-securities-deferrals> Bloomberg <https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ericbalchunas_etf-market-making-had-a-big-year-a-record-share-7408948490925416448-DJr0/>reported last December that Jane Street accounts for 21% of market share for ETF market making while Susquehanna and Citadel Securities account for 14.4% and 11.2% respectively.
Goldman largely exited the ETF market making space in 2017 but made an official return last summer by becoming lead market maker on a new ETF from Capital Group. Bloomberg r <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-07-25/goldman-returns-as-etf-lead-market-maker-after-eight-year-exit>eported at the time that Jane Street is lead market maker on over 800 ETFs. The bank clearly has ambition to close the gap.
The focus on low-latency infrastructure also comes at an interesting time; Hudson River Trading's </news/the-coffee-run-the-kind-trading-firm-paying-1m-to-graduates-and-100m-to-its-top-people>head of AI Iain Dunning told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/audio/2025-10-31/odd-lots-how-hudson-river-trading-actually-uses-ai-podcast>last October that "all the latency has been arbitraged for the most part," suggesting that HFT strategies aren't the gold mine they once were. JPMorgan's burgeoning 'AI Markets Lab' is focused on both high-frequency (seconds or less) and mid-frequency </news/hft-jobs-medium-frequency-trading> (minutes to days) trading strategies. The assets it will be trading aren't as clear, but it will focus on "risk-taking strategies" in addition to market making.
It's not just the banks pushing into this space either; hedge funds want a piece too. In April, </news/millennium-quietly-hired-the-cto-of-a-major-hft-firm-to-work-on-nanosecond-latency-architecture> Millennium hired Alexandre Fournier, former CTO of Tower Research Capital, to run its low-latency tech team: SPEED. Today that division is hiring multiple high frequency trading engineers in Singapore and New York.

item.title: Hedge fund Citadel hired a quant researcher from TGS and gave him a large job
item.description:
As we reported </news/tgs-management-company-llc>earlier this year, electronic trading firm TGS Management LLC is like Wonka's Chocolate Factory to the extent that once people join they rarely come out. Lately, however, one of TGS's long serving quant researchers has emerged blinking into the light and has joined Citadel.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Citadel declined to comment for this article, but writing on LinkedIn, Alexey Poyarkov, a Russian quant researcher who spent over a decade at TGS, said he is now Citadel's head of GQS SCI, a unit in its global quantitative strategies group.
It's not clear when Poyarkov left TGS. It's thought he may have left last year and that he has been on a non-compete. Coincidentally, or not, his arrival follows the decision of Brian Murphy </news/citadel-s-head-of-quantitative-trading-is-now-having-a-rest-for-full-time-parenting>, a senior trader in Citadel's GQS group, to take time out to be with his children.
Poyarkov appears to be a big deal. Before his decade at TGS, he spent time at Google, Microsoft and Yandex. He is a mathematics graduate of Lomonosov Moscow State University, as is the friendly figure of Alex Gerko at XTX. </news/2022/03/russian-quants> The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-quants-run-wall-street-now-1495389108>reported in 2017 that TGS hired Poyarkov as an algorithm designer despite his lack of previous financial services experience and paid him $700k in his first year.
People at TGS rarely say they work for TGS on LinkedIn. When we looked at Poyarkov's profile in May, there was no mention of his previous employer. Now there is.
Although people leave TGS infrequently, exits are not unheard of. Joseph Choi <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/the-billion-dollar-hedge-fund-club-is-about-to-get-bigger-47b965f3> reportedly left around 2023 to form hedge fund JCAP, which appeared to close in 2024. Another trader, Harvard PhD Bo Liu, is thought to have left TGS for Millennium in 2021 before leaving again three years later.

item.title: Citi sent a memo meaning people will need to spend more time in the office
item.description:
Among investment banks </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>, Citi has been fairly relaxed about working from home. In February last year, CEO Jane Fraser </news/jane-fraser-citi-sexism>said <https://www.ft.com/content/12b94232-8d89-4f81-8ac8-df97c9c90106?syn-25a6b1a6=1> that she was all for people working from home two days a week, even while people like Jamie Dimon </news/2021/04/working-from-home-jpmorgan> have railed against it. </news/jamie-dimon-work-from-home>
Nineteen months later, Citi is still letting its people work from home two days a week. But it has slightly tightened the parameters.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In a memo sent earlier this week, Citi informed hybrid staff that starting from October 1st, public holidays globally will no longer count towards in-office days. On weeks with public holidays (eg. Thanksgiving, Christmas, 4th of July in the US), employees will therefore still need to be in the office three days. Previously, employees had been treating these holidays as a reason to come into the office twice.
Citi declined to comment for this article. In sections of the memo seen by eFinancialCareers, Sara Wechter, Citi's head of HR, said: "Beginning October 1, public or national holidays will not count toward your three-day-in-office commitment. During weeks with a paid holiday, please plan to be on-site three days.” Wechter also declared that Citi is proud of its hybrid work model. "It has become a defining part of what makes working at Citi special and the flexibility it provides has helped us retain and attract top talent.”
Some Citi employees are unhappy with the turn of events though. There are suggestions that the new policy could result in people spending an extra two weeks, or more, in the office each year.
Eyebrows have also been raised at the memo's tone. It's understood to have included a warning that employees violating the new requirements will be put on a performance improvement plan. Citi has also launched a new attendance monitoring dashboard and people who attend the office infrequently will find their in-office requirements increase. Citi is always understood to have linked performance to time in the office, but it is becoming more explicit.
Employees fear they will be summoned five days a week from January.

item.title: Wells Fargo's ballooning team of tech bankers hired an MD from UBS
item.description:
Wells Fargo clearly wants to make up for lost time. </news/wells-fargo-md-hiring>After its asset cap was lifted last year, the bank has made significant moves to bolster its investment banking division, particularly within technology banking </news/highest-paid-bankers>. Its latest hire is a New York-based MD who joined from UBS.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Joel Thompson, a medical technology banking specialist, joined Wells Fargo as an MD last week according to FINRA's BrokerCheck tool. He was an MD at UBS since 2023, joining as part of the Credit Suisse acquisition. He was hired by the now-defunct Swiss bank in 2022; Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/credit-suisse-hires-berenberg-analyst-lead-emea-healthcare-investment-banking-2022-01-20/> reported at the time that he covered MedTech as well as 'life science tools and diagnostics.' Before that, Thompson was an MD at both Moelis and Morgan Stanley, specialising in MedTech for both.
Thompson is one of many new faces over the past year. The clear focus is on tech bankers; Jusung 'Juice' Kwok, former head of technology M&A for Deutsche Bank, joined as the bank's global head of semiconductor investment banking in San Francisco. Sarah Kanes, an ex-Mizuho MD, joined late last year as head of data centre banking. At least five other senior tech bankers have joined Wells Fargo this year. </news/technology-bankers#:~:text=Wells%20Fargo%2C%20which%20has%20recruited%20six%20(Badhri%20Varanasi%2C%20Matthew%20Lacy%2C%20Jesse%20Chasse%2C%20Derrick%20Chao%2C%20Jusung%20Juice%20Kwok%2C%20and%20Mark%20Gracia)>
Deal volume in technology is the highest that it has been since 2021 but, for the last few years, Wells Fargo has been nowhere close to the top spots in Dealogic's TMT M&A rankings. </news/highest-paid-bankers>Bringing in these big names can't be cheap; Headhunters say that TMT business heads across banking are on over $10m while heads of subdivisions of tech can be on over $8m.

item.title: The nicest guy in hedge funds is having a hard year. What next for Taula Capital?
item.description:
People who run hedge funds can be intense </news/ken-griffin-citadel-culture>and sometimes volatile. </news/sam-wisnia-eisler-capital-s-deputy-cio-is-looking-to-start-his-own-hedge-fund> They can also be exceptional humans. The two things are not mutually exclusive, but in the London hedge fund universe, no one has a bad word to say about Diego Megia, whose niceness is renowned.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"He's lovely," says one headhunter. "He is a legend," says one portfolio manager. Megia is widely held </news/taula-capital-hedge-fund> to combine talent, humility and approachability. He is a "good person."
It's unfortunate, then, that Megia is having a difficult year. His fund, Taula Capital Management, reportedly fell </news/macro-hedge-fund-managers>9.6% between March 1st and 20th following the outbreak of the Iran war. In early August, Taula had recovered some ground and was down only 5% or so. There are unconfirmed suggestions that it's fallen against since.
Taula's recent performance has not been confirmed by the fund itself, which declined to comment for this article. But given that Taula was founded with $3bn in capital from Millennium, </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium> there has been speculation that Millennium could at some point impose a stop-loss on its share of Taula's circa $8.5bn of assets under management (AUM) if losses worsen. Millennium declined to comment for this article. It's not clear how Millennium treats losses at the external managers it's invested in, but the fund has a reputation for imposing strict conditions on its own portfolio managers. The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/the-giant-hedge-fund-that-hates-risk-and-still-wins-1110e90a> reported in 2024 that Millennium portfolio managers have their capital allocations cut </news/millennium-hedge-fund-loss-index-rebalancing>if they lose 5% and removed entirely if they lose 7.5% or more. One source with knowledge of Millennium's operations said these risk limits can be applied to external managers too.
Millennium's strict approach to losses possibly explains why Taula raised an additional $1.75bn in April, at which point its AUM were reported <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-31/diego-megia-s-hedge-fund-taula-raises-1-75-billion-in-new-cash> to be $8.5bn+. Five months ago, therefore, 65% of Taula's assets were from investors other than the Millennium mother ship. At launch in 2024, 60% of Taula's $5bn in assets came from Millennium.
Megia himself also came from Millennium, where he was a senior portfolio manager for five and a half years, having previously worked for Citadel and Barclays. He founded Taula with 25 other ex-Millennium people, including deputy CIO Stefan Ericsson, whom Millennium allegedly lured from Citadel with a $50m package. </news/london-s-top-new-hedge-fund-has-millennium-s-alleged-50m-man>
Since then, Taula has made additional hires. They include Mehdi Belhachmi, </news/volatility-traders-hedge-funds>a Morgan Stanley volatility trader who was expected to join Goldman Sachs and was being pursued by multiple other funds, but who chose Taula instead last year. Lewis Morton </news/eisler-capital-s-ill-fated-head-of-hr-says-it-was-a-formative-experience>, the former star trader at ill-fated Eisler Capital, also joined Taula in 2025. Both Morton and Ericsson are based in Jersey. </news/lewis-morton-eisler>
Some of Taula's woes in 2026 are externally imposed. The fund is focused on macro trading, </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund> and macro traders have had a challenging year versus funds focused on equities and commodities </news/commodities-trading-hiring-2026>. Taula has been adding portfolio managers in the broader macro space, but it's also been labouring against the long non-competes that elongate the portfolio manager hiring process. Alex McCaffrey, another ex-Barclays trader, for example, joined Taula only in late July 2026, despite leaving Citadel in April 2025.
McCaffrey was a senior portfolio manager at Citadel. When new hires get up to speed, Taula's performance may be expected to improve. The latest performance figures are expected to be released at the end of this month.
In the meantime, there is some whispering among headhunters that some of Taula's PMs might be exploring other options. This is unconfirmed, but it's not difficult to see why this might be the case. Two years ago, Millennium explained </news/millennium-hedge-fund-jobs>what happens there when portfolio managers lose money: "Generally the losses are carried forward and past losses must be made up before performance-based compensation becomes payable in subsequent years..." The implication is that there are no bonuses on Millennium's money until losses are covered.
Some Taula PMs have left already. One left for Jupiter Research Capital in New York in late 2025. Samuele Grosso </news/hsbc-trader-who-left-for-a-hedge-fund-quickly-joins-his-old-boss-at-a-us-bank> went to Bank of America in June '26. Matteo Sardo went to Point72 around the same time.
Taula may yet rebound. Megia's supporters are certain that it will. Other macro hedge funds, like Rokos Capital Management, are also known for their volatility, although Rokos rose during the chaos of March. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-09/macro-trader-chris-rokos-made-money-in-march-as-peers-got-stung> Megia declined to comment for this article, but is said to be running a steady ship.
Megia has funded a foundation <https://www.icr.ac.uk/study-and-careers/working-life-and-benefits/employee-stories/detail/the-cris-cancer-foundation> he set up with his wife to research a cure for cancer after she was diagnosed with multiple myeloma aged 37 in 2008. "Good things happen to good people," says one portfolio manager who knows him. Another claims Megia has recovered from drawdowns in the past. "Diego always comes out on top."
