item.title: Investment bank associates can't even buy "mid tier houses" in London. This is why
item.description:
Banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> was one of the most lucrative careers for young people to break into in previous decades, but the purchasing power of young bankers </news/2023/10/deutsche-bank-london-pay>has significantly declined as costs have risen. This appears to be hitting them hardest when it comes to building wealth through the housing market.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Calculations from Mike Bell, <https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mike-bell-cfa_as-house-prices-move-sideways-and-earnings-share-7508054999114059776-Euwa/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAC_n9ABKGyf486Jq5_52e4WCygx5h9EouQ> head of market strategy at Bluebay Asset Management, show that the purchasing power of dual income couples, each earning £100k, has fallen significantly since 2021.
Bell looked at income after tax and mortgage payments, for a couple on a combined salary of £200k who bought a £1.2m house in 2021, versus a couple buying the same house today on an inflation-adjusted income of £252k.
He found that, if the couples had an interest only mortgage, their yearly spending on mortgage payments would have increased by over £30k. If they had a repayment mortgage, their yearly mortgage spending would have increased by £20k. This took its toll on post-mortgage income, which was down 28% and 20% respectively in real terms.
Source: Mike Bell
In banking, this has been compounded by squeezed pay. Prior to the financial crisis, top banking associates were globally earning the equivalent to $450k+ </news/investment-bank-associates-today-earn-less-than-the-weakest-2007-lehman-brothers-associates> (£336k). Today, data from our compensation and bonus report suggests that the average associate at a tier one investment bank earns closer to $200k (£149.5k) globally.
Lacklustre bonuses are a factor; one junior banker at Morgan Stanley in London told us last year </news/morgan-stanley-s-junior-london-bankers-are-not-happy-with-bonuses>that analysts received 15-30% of their salary as a bonus, compared to 95-100% of salaries in 2021. </news/2021/09/banking-bonuses>
House prices in London, meanwhile, have soared. The average price of a terraced house is £3m in zone one, £1.6m in zone two and £1.1m in zone three. Artem Ponomarev, a fintech founder in London, tweeted in July <https://x.com/apnmrev/status/2081426910236565832>that his friend working as an IB associate could not even afford a "mid tier house" in London.
Renting isn't exactly affordable either. One WallStreetOasis <https://www.wallstreetoasis.com/forum/investment-banking/london-rent-ib-analysts-2025-edition#:~:text=Would%20like%20to,is%20a%20thief)>user complained last year that a one bedroom flat in Aldgate which cost £1.6k in 2021 now costs £3.5k. If the couple on £252k were to stay there while saving up money for a deposit, they'd have more than 20% less income in real terms to save towards that house. This is not including changes to service charges and council tax.
Some bankers are spending less. A diary from Irish publication <https://www.thejournal.ie/readme/money-diaries-spending-saving-66-6851147-Nov2025/>
<http://wa.me/442079977910> </about/editor-tips> <https://unsplash.com/@virginiaphotostories?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText> <https://unsplash.com/photos/a-row-of-brick-buildings-next-to-each-other-QDWvbdD_W5c?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText>

item.title: Morning Coffee: Bank of America's fixed income traders have got some good excuses. How London bankers are boosting their bonuses
item.description:
Last week, Brian Moynihan, the jokey CEO leading Bank of America </news/brian-moynihan-bank-of-america>, said things haven't been going as well at the bank in the third quarter as in the first and second quarters and that fixed income sales and trading revenues in particular have been erratic, if not down. At one point following his speech, BofA's share price fell 6%.
This week, Bank of America's fixed income traders are fighting back.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Speaking to Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-21/bofa-s-slower-ai-ramp-up-is-hitting-the-bank-s-trading-desk>, 'people familiar with the matter' said that because BofA hasn't participated in some of this year's biggest AI debt-issuance deals, it's been harder for them to make the most of the subsequent bond trading activity. It was not their fault.
Whose fault was it then? Maybe Brian's? Maybe BofA's top debt capital markets bankers? Maybe someone like Mike Joo </news/bank-of-america-m-a>, who has a DCM background and who was co-running investment banking but is now off to Barclays instead? Maybe it was just fate.
Either way, BofA is trying to make amends. Having missed out on most of this year's $400bn of debt issuance, BofA is now endeavouring to deploy $250bn of its own capital into "critical infrastructure," including AI infrastructure, between now and next year.
Unfortunately, though, this may come too late to make much difference to this year's BofA fixed income trading bonuses. On the margins, it may even come too late to save some traders' jobs if BofA feels inclined to make any year-end cuts </news/bank-of-america-is-only-replacing-75-of-employees-who-leave>. This is presumably why unnamed people familiar have taken to Bloomberg to proclaim their lack of responsibility.
Bank of America's traders can also find solace in the fact that they are not alone in having a stodgy end to the year. Nomura's traders aren't doing great either <https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/2026/09/17/companies/nomura-slow-growth-warning/>. Nor are Goldman Sachs'. </news/macro-hedge-fund-losses>Goldman has played a key role in financing the AI boom <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/goldman-talks-with-investors-nvidia-financing-deal-after-landing-prized-role-2026-08-14/>, so its traders can't even use BofA traders' excuse. But BofA's unnamed insiders are pointing out that rates and municipal bond trading haven't been great this quarter, either.
Separately, bankers and traders in London have found a method of supplementing/investing bonus payments. Bloomberg reports that they have been buying up the January 2028 gilt.
Purchases of this particular gilt have reportedly risen as much as 50% on retail investing platforms in the past two weeks. It's popular because tax is only paid on its tiny 0.125% coupon and - because it's a gilt - the rest is free from capital gains tax. As it moves towards par at maturity, buyers can benefit from the rise in price. And because it matures in 2028, geopolitical exposure is limited. Bloomberg spoke to "more than a dozen" people on trading floors who said they were buying it. BofA traders could hedge their failings this way, too.
Meanwhile...
Suddenly, the big AI IPOs are on hold. Anthropic was expected to file for an IPO valuing it at $2tn this month. Open AI founder Sam Altman has said floating before next year would be, "ill-advised.” (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/3848a4ad-1426-4352-ba86-ef1279c4ffd1?syn-25a6b1a6=12>
AI IPOs are out, oil tanker IPOs are in. Trafigura is floating its supertanker arm with the intention of raising $500m. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/a1c9d298-8af9-4cf4-9c47-e2eb50cd03d9?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Adnane Ait Omar left Deutsche Bank for Barclays last year. Now he's gone back to Deutsche Bank, where he will be the new global head of FX options platforms. (FX-Markets) <https://www.fx-markets.com/people/7949874/deutsche-bank-hires-from-barclays-for-global-fx-options-role>
Jamie Dimon is going to India. JPMorgan employs 60,000 people there, working in quant research, data science and cloud computing. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-21/dimon-heads-to-india-as-wall-street-steps-up-fight-for-deal-boom?fromMostRead=true>
Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden thinks autonomous AI agents could cause a market meltdown and that kill switches are needed but that we're running out of time to implement them. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-21/boe-s-breeden-says-time-running-out-to-stop-ai-crashing-markets?srnd=homepage-uk>
Citi finished revamping its Canary Wharf tower and is moving in. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-moves-staff-into-canary-wharf-tower-after-1-5bn-revamp-83d6dc81>
Standard Chartered, Citigroup and other banks accidentally handled billions of dollars from a Kremlin-backed fintech company that tricked its way into the global financial system with forged documents. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/3848a4ad-1426-4352-ba86-ef1279c4ffd1?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
KPMG is laying people off and doesn't appear to be offering high severance pay. You get half a week's pay for each year worked while under 22, one week's pay for each year worked from age 22 to 40, and 1.5 weeks' pay for each year worked from age 41. (The Register) <https://www.theregister.com/channel/2026/09/18/kpmg-tech-cuts-come-with-a-severance-sum-some-staff-call-insulting/5296942?utm_source=dlvr.it&utm_medium=twitter>
The new hot skills. Can you recognize patterns? Can you synthesize lots of disparate pieces of information? Can you figure out what perspectives are credible and which ones aren’t? item.title: A French bank managed to get rid of 21,000 employees using gentle techniques
item.description:
If you work for an American investment bank and it wants to cut costs, you may be called into a meeting with HR and then find your access to internal systems is removed.
If you work for a French bank and it wants to cut costs you might be paid your full salary to work part time or given a large voluntary redundancy payment and encouraged to go on your way. Or at least, this is what might happen if you work for SocGen.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
SocGen didn't say anything about its infamously generous voluntary redundancy programme </news/2019/03/socgen-voluntary-redundancy-plan-2019> during today's strategy presentation <https://www.societegenerale.com/sites/default/files/documents/2026-09/capital-markets-day-presentation.pdf>. It did say that it's got rid of 21,000 people across the bank since 2023 and that it's done so using a combination of "natural attrition", "delayering" and cutting back on recruitment while retraining and redeploying its existing people instead.
Voluntary redundancy programmes aren't exactly natural attrition, but SocGen has a strong history of nudging people out the door. Last year, ten material risk takers at the French bank received $1m </news/severance-payments-banks>in each. This was only slightly less than the $1.2m average compensation that SocGen paid the 384 investment banking MRTs who remained employed.
In the past, SocGen has been known to run voluntary redundancy programmes offering one month's salary per six months' service, with minimum payments of €25k (or €50k for employees with more than five years' service). More recently the CFDT Union says <https://www.cfdt-sg.fr/les-informations/accord-emploi-sg-pourquoi-la-cfdt-signe-t-elle/anJ0Ym5zdzdGUHdPbVpHdmhUZ3lGZz09> SocGen has been offering an option of working 80% of the time on full pay for two years at most, and allowing people nearing retirement age to work 50% of the time on 75% on total compensation (including the past two years' average bonuses) for up to three years, too. Next year, it's supplementing this with "external mobility leave" giving people 75% of their pay for six months while they develop a project outside of SocGen.
It's a creative approach and it seems to be working well for the French bank. American banks may want to pay close attention. Bank of America is also attempting to shrink via natural attrition, </news/bank-of-america-is-only-replacing-75-of-employees-who-leave> but SocGen is the master of this art.
Not all SocGen's methods are popular, though. The French bank is also demanding that employees return to the office four days a week, thereby encouraging some people to resign.
Sometimes senior people leave unexpectedly. Francisco Oliveira </news/francisco-oliveira>unexpectedly wafted out of the markets business to pursue other opportunities in July. Oliveira had been co-head of markets and running SocGen's fixed income trading business. SocGen said today that it still has some big aspirations in this area, and wants to expand its fixed income franchise across derivatives, financing and credit.

item.title: Jane Street hired Morgan Stanley's head of US rates sales
item.description:
Proprietary trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm#:~:text=What%20are%20prop,to%20external%20capital.> like Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>don't manage money on behalf of clients but that doesn't mean there isn't a place for salespeople. The electronic trading firm has a sizeable sales and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> division which "work[s] with top institutional investors and asset managers;" it just hired a top rates salesperson from Morgan Stanley to bolster that team.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Lindsay Bofman, Morgan Stanley's head of US rates sales, announced that she is joining Jane Street's sales team in New York. Finra's BrokerCheck tool suggests that her last day at Morgan Stanley was last Friday, and that she hasn't officially started work at Jane Street yet. Bofman spent eight years at Morgan Stanley, making MD in 2021. </news/2021/01/morgan-stanley-managing-directors-2021.-goldman-sachs-intern-complains> Before that, she spent a decade with Barclays, also focused on interest rates sales, having started her career with Lehman Brothers </news/investment-bank-associates-today-earn-less-than-the-weakest-2007-lehman-brothers-associates> in the summer of 2008.
She's not the first sales MD from a bank to join Jane Street. Niamh Taylor, </news/the-ex-emea-head-of-hedge-fund-schonfeld-is-back-at-jane-street> a former MD in prime and alternatives sales for JPMorgan, joined Jane Street in London at the start of last year to work on 'bank and broker management.' She was also previously hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>Schonfeld's head of EMEA.
What exactly will Bofman be selling at Jane Street? The firm did not respond to a request for comment. Jane Street does much more than just algorithmic trading these days; for example, the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/a2dcd05d-2bcd-40a4-adc6-cbbff016222f?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported earlier this month that the firm is now the biggest player in the Asian equities block trading space. Finra reports show that 'Jane Street Capital LLC' <https://brokercheck.finra.org/firm/summary/103782> provides services to multiple major banks; it offers "clearance, custody and other services" to Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan while providing "prime brokerage services" to Wells Fargo, BNP Paribas and Cantor Fitzgerald.

item.title: Another Nomura rates trader has resurfaced at a hedge fund
item.description:
Nomura's macro trading business </news/nomura-experienced-another-singapore-macro-resignation> has had its fair share of senior departures in 2026. Many left after bonuses </news/nomura-paid-its-bonuses-and-now-some-traders-are-leaving>, some left before. Mathias Berenger, a rates options trader, left in February after five years at the bank. Following a six month absence, he's back with a hedge fund. </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Berenger joined Capstone Investment Advisors in London as a portfolio manager. He has held a number of very senior roles in both banks and hedge funds; he was head of US volatility trading at Citi and head of European vanilla options trading across both Credit Suisse and Barclays. He also spent time as a portfolio manager in both Capula and H2O Asset Management.
The FCA register shows that Berenger was a material risk taker for Nomura's UK business from 2021 to 2023. The bank declined to comment, but it appears that he worked for Nomura in an office outside the UK for the latter half of his tenure.
Other senior departures from Nomura's rates team include Hoe Lon Leng </news/now-nomura-s-global-head-of-rates-and-fx-trading-resigned>, the bank's global head of FX and flow rates trading. He joined Singapore macro fund Modular Asset Management, a spinout of Millennium. As we've noted in the past, </news/2022/05/nomura-fx-jobs>Nomura staff are particular desirable among hedge funds as they're encourage to take more proprietary risk

item.title: Citadel & Citadel Securities released some UK accounts. They suggest some things about deferrals there
item.description:
It's the time of year when UK companies file their accounts for 2025. If you're Citadel </news/2022/10/how-to-get-a-job-at-citadel>, the hedge fund, or Citadel Securities </news/citadel-securities-secret-sauce-and-the-2m-pay-premium>, the electronic trading </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> firm, you file a lot of accounts for 2025. Not all of which are out yet.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
So far, Citadel has released accounts for no fewer than four UK entities. These are: Citadel Management (Europe) III Limited (a provider of services in support of investment management, including trading algorithm and software development, to Citadel companies); Citadel Enterprise Technology Services Ltd. (a provider of technology services to Citadel companies); Citadel HF Management (Europe) LLP (a provider of investment management services to Citadel companies) and Citadel Enterprise Europe Services Ltd. (a provider of risk monitoring and admin services to Citadel companies).
So far, Citadel Securities has released one set of UK accounts. These are for Citadel Securities Europe Services Ltd, which provides algorithm development, technology, trade support and portfolio management to Citadel Securities companies.
Exciting. Except that both companies have yet to release the critical sets of accounts which show what's been going on at their critical UK entities. These are due...soon.
In the meantime, the array of accounts filed so far are not without revelations. Most interestingly, they indicate how it is that people at Citadel and Citadel Securities get paid.
At Citadel, the accounts say that members of the partnership hold capital in a scheme that invests in three funds in the Cayman Islands. These funds (CEIF International, CEIF Partners International and the Citadel Voluntary Investment Fund) return money to partners either when they leave or when the partnership is dissolved. Last year, $156.8m of these payments (made in the form of shares in related companies) were made to partners at Citadel HF Management (Europe) LLP. It's not clear how many people received the $156.8m, but four partners left during the year according to Companies House. These payments were unrelated to the fund's performance.
At one of Citadel's support arms (Enterprise Europe Services), the accounts say that part of people's bonus is invested in Citadel's employee investment funds and that another part is a notional award that tracks a hypothetical investment in certain funds. This notional award vests over a 40 month period.
In Citadel's investment services arms, pay can be deferred for up to 40 months too. At the nattily named Citadel Management (Europe) III, for example, $116.9m of compensation was payable at year end 2025, of which $91.1m was due within three months; $20.1m was due in 3 to 12 months; and $5.6m was due after a year. Deferrals </news/hedge-fund-bonus> take one of three forms: investments in employee funds; notional awards based upon the performance of the hypothetical investment funds; or "participation units" based on the performance of a specific team.
At Citadel Securities, a separate company in the Citadel universe, things are different again. Here, the accounts released so far for Citadel Securities Europe Services Ltd., indicate that employees don't always get equity but instead get deferred cash bonuses that depend upon how other elements of the company perform.
Some of these deferred cash bonuses at Citadel Securities track changes in the EBITDA of other Citadel Securities entities. Others are tied to the value of notional equity in other Citadel Securities companies. These awards generally carry no conditions of service beyond the year they relate to, but recipients can forfeit the payments under unspecified conditions. Either way, though, it seems that Citadel Securities isn't necessarily handing out equity: both payments take the form of cash.
Citadel and Citadel Securities have not commented for this article.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Rebellious equity derivatives trader in shiny shoes is worth $33bn. How to make your MD retire
item.description:
The world is full of traders who have stayed in banks and traders who have left for hedge funds. But there are also traders who have left to set up their own companies and to become multibillionaires. This category includes Alex Gerko </news/alex-gerko-xtx-tax>at XTX. It also includes Nik Storonsky of Revolut.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Revolut and Storonsky have been in the news for two wrong reasons lately. There is something about a yacht, <https://www.ft.com/content/7dd21b1e-3b3d-48a6-a3fe-6a0e4a14944b?syn-25a6b1a6=1> which Storonsky denies. There is something about Revolut leaking data to hackers who pretended to be members of the Italian government and then demanded a $3m ransom. <https://www.ft.com/content/d1f2c9bd-26ce-4e87-9da4-fe0238bd531d?syn-25a6b1a6=1>Neither of these is dwelt upon in the FT's new interview with Storonsky, which opens with his shiny shoes.
Storonsky's shoes are reportedly "the shiniest shoes imaginable." They are paired with a black suit, </news/banking-md-bespoke-tailored-suit> which means Storonsky wouldn't fit in at Goldman Sachs, where navy blue suits </news/goldman-sachs-dress-code>are the thing. But Storonsky wouldn't want to work for Goldman Sachs because he is worth $33bn having founded app-based-fintech-bank Revolut, which is valued at $115bn.
Storonsky used to be an equity derivatives trader. He saved his bonuses to start Revolut. His time at Credit Suisse and Lehman has been well-documented and is credited with his enthusiasm for 13 hour days and working weekends. </news/why-working-for-revolut-founder-nik-storonsky-is-a-pleasure>But the FT says his experience at the failed banks also drove an intense risk aversion that might explain why Storonsky has gone for smart shoes as he considers an IPO. <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/revolut-plans-dual-listing-new-york-london-french-newspaper-les-echos-reports-2026-09-17/>
At Lehman Brothers, the trading book could be down "millions of dollars within one day," says Storonsky. At Credit Suisse, infighting and politics were debilitating. At Revolut, Storonsky says he's trying to build something much more solid and much less risky. Most notably, while most banks lend 100% of their deposits, Revolut is only lending 6%. It doesn't plan to lend more than 10-20%, says Storonsky. And when Revolut does lend these amounts, the loans will be sold on outright or displaced through securitisations.
Storonsky is an ex-trader who doesn't like risk. He does like kite-surfing, which he says is like meditation. He doesn't dress like a surfer so much now. If he wanted, he could buy a lot of shoe polish.
Separately, now that adult children can't afford to live without parental assistance, managing directors in banks are hanging around and failing to retire. </news/fire-banking-mds>
The WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/business/law-firms-retirement-incentives-packages-1e9bccbd?mod=hp_lead_pos3> says top law firms have the same problem and are filling up with partners in their late 50s, and older.
However, the WSJ says there is also a way to persuade these people to cede their positions to the next generation. Law firms have been hiring consultants to help nudge people out the door, and these consultants are asking questions like, "How many healthy years do you have left in your life, and what do you plan to do with them, thinking two years at a time?"
In this way, the WSJ says it's been possible to persuade partners to leave and do things like work on a revival of the Rocky Horror Show instead.
Meanwhile...
Warren Buffett's son has been made chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. This doesn't seem right. He was previously a farmer, a member of local government and a director of Berkshire and some other public companies. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/9f3fd7bc-ca51-4401-8f63-b6b25e88621f?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
OpenAI is hiring 200 people in Singapore. Anthropic is opening an office there. DeepMind and Mistral each plan to have 100 people there by the end of the year. Databricks has 250 people and is expanding. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/775888b2-47e6-42b4-8146-cfb9caee52d6?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Shares in Goldman Sachs fell 7% last week. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/3bb7e0e8-6aef-4b6b-a5f0-f472a2655c1f?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Citadel Securities has a 24-hour US equities trading service and now has about 10 people in Hong Kong focused on sales and servicing these clients, and about 50 in the US. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-17/citadel-securities-taps-asia-sovereign-funds-for-24-hour-trading?taid=6aaba3dd4ca3b500013d3bb7&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
The Bank of England and the Fed are scrutinising trading firms after Jane Street lost $15bn in July. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/f1d9d398-0666-44cf-96f4-390e6c3f5173?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Jonathan Raiff was running fixed income for Verition. Now he's going to Schonfeld. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-18/hedge-fund-verition-s-fixed-income-head-jonathan-raiff-exits?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260918&utm_campaign=author_22884492>
Andy Burnham might increase UK capital gains tax to 45% in order to raise the income tax threshold to £16k. (Telegraph) <https://www.telegraph.co.uk/money/tax/capital-gains/burnham-weighs-14bn-capital-gains-tax-raid/>
When students ask broadly for information about a career, female students receive substantially more information on work/life balance than male students. (NBER) <https://www.nber.org/papers/w35750>
A drill rig that was solidifying the foundation of Citadel’s new Miami office fell onto three cars. Four people went to hospital. Work has stopped. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/real-estate/ken-griffins-new-miami-headquarters-on-pause-after-construction-accident-3ea3b5af?mod=hp_lead_pos6>
Hilton (hotels) received 4,000 applications for 20 places on its early careers program. (Fortune) <https://fortune.com/2026/09/20/hilton-applications-gen-zers-internships-early-career-program-chro-ai-hospitality-jobs/>
“Adverse workplace developments” such as “organizational restructuring, worsening management practice, performance pressures, heightened workload, or internal conflict,” are bad for your mental health long before you're actually fired. (Rob Henderson) <https://www.robkhenderson.com/p/your-job-gives-you-more-than-money?utm_source=substack&publication_id=800237&post_id=213141633&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>
“I want that job at Goldman. I will take it for any title, any role, and any pay. I will work in the mail room. But first, I want to interview at all those other banks you mentioned. Those will be my practice rounds. By the time I get to Goldman, I will be an expert witness up there on the stand.” (NoRebates) <https://norebates.substack.com/p/cracking-the-code?utm_source=substack&publication_id=744072&post_id=215772803&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>

item.title: "I work in electronic trading. I come to the office once a quarter"
item.description:
I am very lucky. I work for an electronic trading business based in New York City, but I do not live or work in New York City. I live miles outside and I come into the office as little as possible.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
These days, I usually come into the office once a quarter. It wasn't always like this. Before the pandemic, I was in the office every day. Then I moved further out. I've never come back.
This suits me. The rest of my team are in the office, but one other guy and I held out. It makes no sense for us to come to the office. We're both introverts and we both spend all our time on screens anyway, even when we do make the slog into Manhattan.
Initially we were also working with guys in India, but they've been dumped since we discovered AI could do their work instead. I feel quite secure in my role because I know I have the experience that would make me hard to replace.
I make sure that I work hard. At the very least, this is an 8-5 job, but I work more than that. The best thing about continuing to work from home is that I'm able to stop work and immediately do some exercise every day. In the past, I'd just be sitting on a train.
Now I'm forced to find local things near my home that I can do outside of work. When I do go into the office I make sure to meet with all the team. It works for me - I think partly because they know I'd resign if they tried to make me come back to the office full-time.
Adam Mangels is a pseudonym

item.title: Some top Squarepoint traders joined big funds. Now they're leaving again
item.description:
Squarepoint, the quantitative </news/biggest-quant-hedge-funds> hedge fund, </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> is sometimes compared to Qube Research and Technologies. </news/qube-research-and-technologies-has-been-hiring-heavily-paying-less>Both are run by the French. </news/2021/03/french-quants-banking> Both spun out of banks. Based on our admittedly partial visibility, though, it seems that people might leave Squarepoint more frequently.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Squarepoint's past departures include Nathan Benabou, a top quant portfolio manager (PMs) who left in 2021 and joined Point72 in Dubai, and Khalil Bouchareb </news/hedge-fund-millennium-has-quietly-been-hiring-people-from-squarepoint>, one of Squarepoint's top PMs, who went to Millennium in early 2025.
We understand that Benabou has left Point72 and is enroute elsewhere. Some members of his seven person team are understood to have left too, although some have been redeployed at Point72.
Similarly, we understand that Khalil Bouchareb will be leaving Millennium along with Antoine Le Calvez, a quant researcher who also formerly worked for Squarepoint. Bouchareb's intention is unclear; it's understood that he's still at Millennium at the moment.
Point72 and Millennium declined to comment. Benabou didn't respond to a request to comment.
Benabou is thought to have been among the top performers at Cubist, Point72's systematic investing business. Cubist has been through a few changes </news/hedge-fund-point72-lost-one-of-its-top-quant-researchers>. In late 2025, Point72 hired Geoffrey Lauprete, <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-09-10/point72-replaces-cubist-chief-with-ex-worldquant-cio-lauprete>the former CIO of WorldQuant to run Cubist, thereby displacing Denis Dancanet. It's thought that Dancanet hired Benabou. Issam Bazzi, another senior quant on the team, was reported to leave in March. Lauprete has been hiring his own people to Cubist, including - most recently - John Koehl from Balyasny. Benabou's departure may have been prompted by these changes.
Meanwhile, Squarepoint itself has been doing some hiring. Recent recruits to its team include macro portfolio manager Mark Orsley in New York (ex-BlueCrest) and Priyanka Chatterjee (ex-Verition). Squarepoint didn't respond to a request to comment.

item.title: Three equities MDs are leaving UBS in London. One is leaving for a new role
item.description:
As we reported </news/ubs-cuts-hiring> earlier this week, UBS still has costs to cut before the end of this year. It's not clear whether this is why senior people in its electronic equities business have been leaving, but in the case of at least one departure the exit is understood to have been entirely voluntary.
UBS isn't commenting, but it's understood that Chris Marsh, global head of electronic and program trading, Michael Farthing, head of global markets execution technology, and Irina Sonich-Bright, head of market access and agency trading are all leaving.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Neither Marsh, Farthing nor Sonich-Bright responded to a request to comment.
It's understood that Sonich-Bright resigned and is joining a fintech firm after a period of gardening leave. The intentions of Marsh and Farthing are unclear.
Colleagues said the exit of Marsh in particular is a shock. "He is very, very senior," said one. Marsh and Farthing are expected to appear in new roles soon. "They are a big loss for UBS," said another former colleague.
All three joined UBS from Credit Suisse and previously worked on Credit Suisse's advanced execution services (AES) trading product. Both Marsh and Farthing arrived prior to the shotgun wedding. Following this event, UBS was reported </news/2023/08/credit-suisse-ubs-unwanted-people> to have turned off key elements of the AES system in 2023.
UBS isn't thought to have retained many of the Credit Suisse AES people. There are now fears that remaining people like Jonathan Tse </news/2023/10/credit-suisse-to-ubs-algorithmic-trading>could leave too. They could always go and work for Naz Al-Khudairi </news/popular-london-electronic-trading-head-has-a-big-new-job-and-money-to-hire>, the former star of AES who is currently building a team at Ingenuity Trading.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Hedge fund explains why its $10m+ ex-Citi MD is so special. HSBC's Hong Kong bankers may be less fecund in the future
item.description:
Once they join Citi, people don't always appear to leave again. </news/wall-street-experience>But George Saghir joined Citi in 1985 and left again as an MD 11 years later. George is still going and is now the subject of a battle between big hedge funds. </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>
Saghir has been working for ExodusPoint, the macro-focused multistrategy hedge fund </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund>founded by Michael Gelband. But he would like to work for Schonfeld, the hedge fund run by the youthful Ryan Tolkin, who is always prepared for meetings </news/hedge-fund-schonfeld-s-ceo-suggests-ai-will-mostly-eliminate-data-jobs>. Saghir wants to work for Schonfeld so much, that he has joined the fund six weeks before he's supposed to.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-17/exoduspoint-sues-ex-portfolio-manager-for-starting-at-schonfeld?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260917&utm_campaign=author_3487187>reports that Saghir joined Schonfeld on September 2nd. But ExodusPoint has him under a one year non-compete </news/citadel-non-compete> that's due to end only on October 18th. And ExodusPoint is not happy about Saghir's premature arrival.
In a suit <https://assets.bwbx.io/documents/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/r0FfveGsz6rw/v0> filed against Saghir in the Supreme Court of New York, ExodusPoint details why Saghir is so special. He is a "highly specialized Portfolio Manager," says ExodusPoint. He has "unique investment judgment and capital deployment expertise." He is, "specialized in taking positions on broad macroeconomic and geopolitical trends spanning multiple asset classes and geographies."
Most importantly, ExodusPoint says Saghir is particularly good at developing trading strategies "in response to public economic announcements, such as the publication of non-farm payroll (“NFP”) numbers, consumer price index (“CPI”) data, and Federal Reserve announcements." There have been significant announcements recently and, ExodusPoint feels particularly aggrieved. Now that Saghir is working again, he'll be able to trade against the release of September's economic data in early October, says ExodusPoint. Worse, ExodusPoint says it may be obliged to trade against him.
It's not clear how Saghir feels about this. We have not spoken to him and he didn't respond to Bloomberg's request to comment. However, having your talents aired in public is surely no bad thing. Over the circa 3.5 years that he actually worked there, ExodusPoint says it paid Sahir "tens of millions of dollars." It also says Saghir negotiated </news/hedge-fund-contract> an increase in his "incentive rate" which lifted his compensation in return for extending his non-compete from six to nine months.
ExodusPoint says it's been paying Saghir's salary during his non-compete period and will continue to do so until October. Saghir, who lives in Larchmont, a village north of New York City, and who was recently seen selling a Tudor-style mansion with a pool and kitchen island, <https://www.mansionglobal.com/articles/gwyneth-paltrow-flick-the-perfect-murder-inspired-the-kitchen-reno-in-this-historic-new-york-manor-bc8d21c9>presumably wanted to get back to work.
Schonfeld didn't comment for Bloomberg's article. It clearly likes hiring extremely talented macro portfolio managers and was also recently involved in a dispute with Millennium after attempting to poach Adam Grunfeld </news/hedge-fund-employment-contract>, whom it described as possessing "unique investment judgment, strategy design, and capital deployment expertise developed over many years." Grunfeld never worked for Citi, but began his career at Balyasny </news/balyasny-hedge-fund>in 2004.
Separately, if you work for HSBC in Hong Kong and are thinking of producing many children then think again.
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/3edfa4b0-a492-4627-b9ac-e6f11583242d?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reports that HSBC was paying $38k in school fee subsidies for new hires at director level and above in Hong Kong, partly to attract people to work there. It won't be doing that any more.
Fortunately, HSBC's Hong Kong employees who already have large families can still benefit from the perk. So can Hong Kong employees with children due in 2026. All others will need to pay the fees themselves.
The changes come after HSBC altered its hierarchy five years ago </news/2021/07/hsbc-new-hierarchy> so that some of its lavish perks at the time (first class airline travel and fancy accommodation in Hong Kong along with big pay rises) would be available to fewer people thereafter.
Meanwhile...
Barclays wants people back in the office from three days a week (instead of two) from next month. Barclays staff with commutes longer than 40 minutes would like to be exempt from this edict. People would also like to commute at off-peak times and to receive a payment to offset the extra costs. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/ca551e46-8ced-4e63-ace1-bdf20caedce7?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Nomura says equities trading has been solid, that FX and emerging markets revenues have recovered, but that rates trading has been "challenging." (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-16/nomura-signals-trading-revenue-growth-is-slowing-as-boom-cools>
Now that rates are rising, Apollo thinks some private equity firms might shrink. “I do think you will see a squeezing of the number of managers and maybe some managers that grew really rapidly over the last decade will have to contract back down.” (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/rising-rates-will-make-private-equitys-bad-year-a-lot-worse-255daf59?mod=mhp>
JPMorgan appears to be limiting some engineers to Claude budgets of $2k a month. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/jpmorgan-claude-spending-limit-security-engineers-2026-9>
Revolut is planning a dual listing in New York and London. This is why. “It’s a larger market. It includes institutional investors, hedge funds, fund managers and a considerable number of individual investors.” (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/ee1b5a66-24f2-49b8-b26f-895644ebe3f1?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Revolut's Nik Storonsky bought a €350 million superyacht with a cryotherapy chamber this year. A yacht broker says he owes it €17.5m in commissions. Storonsky says this is not so. (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/revolut-nik-storonsky-superyacht-brokerage-jbl8l0dgp>
Backdoor references are a bigger thing in the age of AI applications. "I heard about a man whose candidacy was doomed by a thumbs-down from his stepmother, who worked in the same industry." (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/articles/more-companies-use-backdoor-job-references-to-counter-ai-fb334e28?st=LhVP3T&reflink=article_copyURL_shar>
Now that AI is about, Kim Posnett, co-head of investment banking at Goldman Sachs, has been telling people to 'lean into apprenticeship acceleration, and focus on distinctly human qualities that matter in business.' (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/goldman-sachs-kim-posnett-investment-banking-ai-use-junior-analysts-2026-9>
The SEC is interviewing current and former employees of Guggenheim Investments as they scrutinise the CEO's business empire. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-17/guggenheim-staff-face-sec-interviews-in-probe-of-walter-s-empire?srnd=homepage-uk>
After making money on the SpaceX IPO, one 35-year-old SpaceX employee and his wife are having a "year of freak" and spending $25k a month on travel and things like acting classes. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/business/spacex-ipo-payouts-41e64c45?mod=mhp>

item.title: A global showcase for Hong Kong careers in London
item.description:
The global super connector city
This is an extremely busy time for Hong Kong business community, and a correspondingly hot hiring market. Last year, Hong Kong was the number one IPO market in the world, and so far in 2026, fundraising has more than doubled from that peak. There have been more than a hundred new issues in the first eight months of the year, with HK$342.4bn (US$43.7bn) raised. The city’s investment banks, technology firms and other industries are reaching out to the rest of the world to maintain their access to global talent.
As well as Hong Kong’s own thriving market, the city is a gateway to the Greater Bay Area of China. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou innovation cluster was ranked first in World Intellectual Property Organization’s Global Innovation Index in both 2025 and 2026. The career opportunities in this economically dynamic area are also supported by Hong Kong’s strong performance in the IMD World Talent Ranking, where it rose to fourth place globally last year — among the highest in Asia.
Hong Kong’s role as a super connector stems from its "One Country, Two Systems" principle, which combines deep collaboration with Chinese Mainland and a globally trusted business environment. Backed by a common‑law framework, world‑class professional services and a simple, competitive tax regime, the city offers an ideal base for executives seeking international exposure and regional growth.
In Hong Kong, rapid growth in local and regional markets, together with an entrepreneurial culture, means promotions and personal development can happen at an accelerated pace. That faster pace of learning is set to become an even greater advantage in the AI era. Hong Kong’s unique culture also helps professionals adapt their skills and capabilities to the changing needs, a period spent in Hong Kong has therefore long been a way to fast-track an international career.
However, many professionals are intimidated by the prospect of relocating to a different financial centre. As well as all of the normal stress and risk of making any job move, there is a need to find housing and make arrangements for family members, along with navigating the visa and residence system. And it can often be daunting to move outside one’s “comfort zone”, trading an established social and career network for an entirely new environment.
Attracting talent, investing in people
In Hong Kong, dedicated support available for global talent. Hong Kong Talent Engage (HKTE), reaches out to international talent, promotes various talent attraction measures, and provides comprehensive services from networking opportunities to relocation guidance, to help them settle in and integrate into the local community.
Paul Moody, Managing Director at CFA Institute, who relocated from London to Hong Kong this year, has made this journey and has first-hand experience of HKTE’s support. He was invited to speak at the Global Talent Summit Week organised by HKTE in March 2026, and has noted that the openness of the network has widened his own connections, spanning different companies, with people offering advice and help regardless of seniority.
For his professional development, Hong Kong offers something he could not find elsewhere, specifically its two-way connectivity. In his words: “No other global financial centre offers the same access to the Chinese Mainland. That gives you unique access into China as a bridge, while remaining connected to international markets.”
On living and working in the city, he notes that day‑to‑day life feels familiar yet offers distinct advantages. “Nothing is significantly different from London, but there are many benefits I didn’t have in London,” he said, citing Hong Kong’s efficient transport, vibrant food scene, a well‑established diversified cultural community and other diverse groups that make settling in straightforward. “In Hong Kong you are pulled into the community from day one, in a good way,” he added.
Photo shows Paul Moody speaking at the Global Talent Summit Week organised by HKTE in March.
A showcase for global talent
One way in which HKTE reaches out to global talent is by organising careers fairs and showcases, to allow professionals who might be considering the next stage in their career to contact employers and learn about opportunities. As well as online events, these showcases are organised in some of the world’s biggest and most important talent markets, to facilitate in-person contact with professionals and graduates who might otherwise not be able to make the trip to Hong Kong. A recent showcase in Malaysia partnered with over 40 enterprises from Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area of China, attracting more than 4,000 visits and 1,000 CVs.
Now, the HKTE talent showcase is coming to London. In a three-part programme taking place over two days on the 17th and 18th of October, more than 50 leading enterprises from Hong Kong and the Chinese Mainland across Banking and Finance, I&T, Engineering and Construction, and other professional services, will come to the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in Westminster.
As well as direct engagements at a careers fair, with CV drop-offs for over 200 immediate job opportunities, the showcase will include forum discussions between experts on the talent landscape and market trends, plus first-hand stories from global professionals who have already made the move. There will also be workshops with practical advice and career tips.
This event will benefit established professionals pursuing international career moves, as well as entrepreneurs and start‑up founders looking to scale. University students and recent graduates will also meet representatives from the region’s leading enterprises. A free executive photography booth will also be available, subject to a limited quota. Participants who complete the specified mission will be eligible for a professional portrait to enhance their CV.
If you are interested in exploring opportunities in one of the most dynamic markets in the fastest growing region in the world, join the “Hong Kong Global Talent & Career Showcase @London”, to meet leading employers and discover new prospects for your career or start-up.
As Paul Moody put it, “The opportunity and the doors are open, but there is a sense that it is a bigger step than it actually is. People imagine it is scarier and more daunting than the reality. A lot of people say they would love to do something like this. If you would love to do it, why not do it?”
Details of the event are available on its dedicated website <https://www.hkengage.gov.hk/en/events/london-career-showcase-2026>.Click here to register now <https://www.hkengage.gov.hk/en/events/london-career-showcase-2026/registration-form?utm_source=efin&utm_medium=website&utm_campaign=uk_showcase_affi> and get ready to make the first steps on a career journey to the most exciting city for global talent.

item.title: Macro hedge funds may have made large losses (again). Only JPMorgan traders are thriving
item.description:
It's been a big week in macro trading. With resurgent inflation and the straitened situation in the Strait and its surroundings, the Fed hiked rates for the first time in three years. The Bank of England didn't, but it suggested hikes are coming. The market is awash with chatter that at least one large hedge fund was wrongly positioned for what has transpired.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Far be it for us to speculate on which large hedge fund this might be. There are suggestions smaller London macro funds may have come unstuck too. Losses this week are said to be in the region of hundreds of millions of dollars.
Macro hedge funds lost money in March, </news/macro-hedge-fund-managers> when funds like Caxton, Taula and Brevan Howard's Master Fund fell 15%, 9.6% and 6% in the month in the immediate fallout from the Iranian war. Many then bounced back. The Brevan Howard Master Fund was up 3.7% <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-05-21/stocks-help-brevan-macro-hedge-fund-offset-rates-trading-losses>in the year through to May. In early August Taula was still down, but by a lesser 5%.
As US treasury yields rise, running a hedge fund becomes more difficult. Citadel CEO Ken Griffin said in May </news/ken-griffin-hedge-fund> that investors are looking for returns "equivalent to the risk free cost of capital, plus 4%." At current rates, funds returning less than 8% are unlikely to be popular destinations for investment.
While macro funds lick their wounds, fixed income traders in banks are also having third quarter angst. Both Bank of America and Goldman Sachs explicitly said this week that fixed income trading revenues had softened versus the first half. Only JPMorgan was explicitly ebullient. There has been "broad-based strength across FICC and equities," said Douglas Petno, CEO of the commercial and investment bank, in reference to Q3.

item.title: AI is steamrolling recruitment firms. They are fighting back with more AI
item.description:
We’ve looked at AI a lot over the years, but especially recently. How AI is changing M&A </news/ai-in-ma-banking>. How it’s changing private equity </news/ai-changing-private-equity>. How it’s changing operations </news/ai-in-operations>. But how exactly is AI changing financial services recruitment itself? Well, it’s complicated.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
We spoke to Kimberley Roe, head of change and transformation IT (permanent) recruitment at UK-based recruitment consultancy Huxley. She tells us that the firm’s London office alone (and it has 55 of them) receives some 800 fresh CVs </news/the-absolutely-perfect-investment-banking-cv> per day – and filters out around 90% of them.
“I would estimate that 600 to 700 of them have been sent using an AI model,” Roe says, “where AI has helped write the CV or someone's using the AI program to send their CV to absolutely everything.” Huxley, in turn, uses an AI application to rank the CVs on how good they are.
Huxley’s AI penalizes your AI. “How can we actually know anything about you?” Roe asks. “The reason you get penalized for AI is it's not your own work.”
You should take heart from the fact that your CV, even if it is a bit miserable, is tenfold better than most AI-written ones. Roe gives the example of a job application for a second-line support role (basically, a bank tech job that involves solving more complex issues than “my laptop no work”), which might receive 10 CVs that are the same. “The whole CV is exactly, word for word, the same,” Roe says. “It means, straight away, we know that's not a legitimate CV, and we can't represent those people to our clients.”
So, what can you do aside from putting a modicum of effort into your CV? You write more and better cover letters. “When CVs are so generic, your cover letter is what can help personalise you, and AI is a really good tool for that,” Roe explains. “Cover letters are more important now.” Of course, writing your cover letter with AI is fine. That should go without saying.
At the end of the day, AI is just another part of the evolution of the recruitment industry. “Our industry will always change, and it needs to change,” Roe says. “When I joined in 2007, it wasn't that long since CVs were still being sent by post or by fax machine.” In turn, sending CVs over the internet was a revolution. “Then CRM systems started to pop up, where clients were using kind of their own portals for us to update people,” Roe says. “That seemed quite revolutionary.” And then there were video interviews, which were just as revolutionary.
Now it is AI. “Businesses on both sides are having to adapt to that; there will always be change,” Roe says. And unlike with other revolutions, AI has a counterrevolutionary element; it “could really help someone in their job search, or it could absolutely destroy it.”
Kimberley Roe will be hosting an ask me anything (AMA) on the bubble, our forum for financial services professionals, on 22 September.

item.title: Salaries and Bonuses in Quant Finance: broken down by role, seniority & region
item.description:
If you're looking for a job in quant finance, </news/quant-jobs-finance> chances are you're after one of the coveted and high-paying quantitative researcher </jobs/quantitative-research> roles. Not everyone can get those, </news/ai-will-only-eat-your-graduate-quant-job-if-you-re-uncreative> however, so what is compensation like in the broader quant finance ecosystem?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The Certificate in Quantitative Finance program (CQF) recently released a 2026 careers guide to quantitative finance <https://www.cqf.com/cqf-careers-guide-quantitative-finance>, containing average salary and total compensation (TC) ranges for multiple roles. We compared this year's figures to those in 2024 and found that pay has risen for every role and every seniority on a global scale. It's a good time to be a quant but, as always, it's particularly good to be a quant in America; the most senior quant researchers </news/what-is-a-quant-researcher-hedge-fund> make an average total compensation of ~$700k, up from $650k in 2024. Even junior quants can expect total compensation over $300k.
Pay has risen for researchers at a faster rate than for quant developers. </news/quant-developer-jobs-in-banking> As AI causes roles to converge, those developers are under threat from both sides; AI-assisted researchers could assume their more quant-y responsibilities while AI-assisted software engineers </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing> can take on their more technical tasks. It's particularly bad to be a quant developer in Asia and Europe; there, researchers earn almost double the total compensation at each level of seniority. In Europe, quant development directors make $270k while quant research directors make $643k.
Pay in Asia is generally much lower for all quant roles but there are some bright spots. Quant risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank>pay has risen massively, with mid-level risk people now able to expect almost 50% more compensation. At director level, risk staff in Asia earn slightly more than those in Europe.
Data science, </news/2020/09/difference-between-a-data-scientist-and-a-quant>which also includes machine learning and AI engineering roles, is more of a mixed bag. In Europe, data science directors make more than quant developers while, in America, they earn almost $100k less.

item.title: The most common LeetCode questions in banks, hedge funds and trading firms
item.description:
A technical job in financial services </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank> is rarely achieved without completing a LeetCode-style </news/leetcode-for-banking-jobs> assessment of some sort. There are thousands of LeetCode questions you could practice to prepare for this interview </news/70-top-banking-interview-questions-and-how-to-answer-them>stage, but some are more common than others.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We've analyzed 576 unique LeetCode questions asked by 31 different financial services firms*. The question that appeared more than any other was one directly relevant to finance: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock. <https://leetcode.com/problems/best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock/> It was asked by nine out of fourteen banks, four out of eight hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>and one of eight electronic trading firms. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>The firms that ask this question most often are Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan and Citadel.
Different firms will have their favourites. Not included in the top ten is Trapping Rain Water, </news/2023/02/goldman-sachs-leetcode-problem> a question known to be a favourite of Goldman Sachs. The question has also been asked by multiple hedge funds including D.E. Shaw and Squarepoint.
The spread of easy, medium and hard-ranked questions differs between sectors. The proportion of hard questions asked by hedge funds is almost double that of banks. Curiously, electronic trading firms </news/difference-between-electronic-trading-firms> ask the highest proportion of easy questions; interviews there often have multiple technical stages </news/high-frequency-trading-internship#:~:text=What%20is%20the,honesty%20are%20key.> including a more complex system design stage, so the easier questions may be a conscious decision to cast a wider net. The average acceptance rate (the percentage of programs submitted that are successful) is roughly the same in each sector at around 55-58%.
How much LeetCode do you need to do to get a job in finance?
AI coding tools </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing> have cast a lot of doubt on the efficiency of LeetCode questions as a tool to filter out candidates. Some would say they were never useful in the first place. The amount of LeetCode you'll need to practice most likely correlates to the volume of LeetCode questions asked by the firm you want to apply for; Goldman Sachs asked the most unique LeetCode questions of any firm we analyzed, and a 2024 study found </news/how-much-leetcode-should-you-do-to-work-at-google-or-goldman-sachs>that Goldman employees had solved an average of 452 questions.
You don't need to be particularly 'cracked' at solving problems either. That 2024 study found that employees at JPMorgan, which asks the second most unique questions, had an average score of 1,500, </news/leetcode-for-banking-jobs> the starting score for new LeetCode users. Goldman Sachs had a marginally greater average score of 1,602.
Recruiters have suggested that, for roles in hedge funds and trading firms, there has been an increased emphasis on non-technical interview stages for technical roles in a post-AI world. Peter Wagner, managing director of recruitment firm Affinity North, said earlier this year </news/the-questions-most-candidates-neglect-in-quant-trading-job-interviews> that behavioural (culture fit) interviews have "grown in importance" and that you "don’t want to make up your answers to behavioral questions on the spot." If you're already above average at LeetCode, reaching out to employees at the firm you want to join or researching the culture might be a more productive use of your time.

item.title: The most experienced people appear to be at Citi. The least experienced appear to be at Goldman
item.description:
What’s an average banker? It’s hard to pin down. And it very much depends on the bank you are working for.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Luckily, data from the Financial Industry Regulation Authority (FINRA) can help. FINRA tracks the number of registered brokers employed by every registered financial services firm in the USA, breaks them down by location, and gives them a brief job history. Taking those figures, we can estimate the average years of experience that any given banker has at any given firm in the USA.
FINRA’s data tells us that the least experienced New York-based bankers are by some margin at Goldman Sachs. Goldman’s employees average just 8.3 years of registered-broker experience, compared to Citi and Bank of America, where they average around 10. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley sit between those two extremes.
Goldman's average is low because FINRA data suggests it employs a high proportion of juniors – people with up to three years of experience. These are essentially analysts </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> and first year associates. 40% of Goldman’s FINRA-registered workforce are at this level, compared to 33% at Citi, the other extreme.
In the four to six years of experience column, which mainly tracks associates </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>, Goldman is not particularly represented. The firm has 15.4% of its registered New York workforce in this camp, compared to the five-bank average of 15.2%. The biggest banks here are Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, whose “associate” workforce are around 16.5% of the total.
Above the six-year mark, and especially between seven years and 15 years, things are more complicated. Most registered professionals at this stage are vice presidents </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> (VPs) or directors </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>. No banks are particularly overweight on this experience level.
When looking at professionals with more than 16 years of experience, and especially those with more than 20 years, things become more complicated. At this stage of their career, a registered professional can reasonably be expected to be a managing director </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> (or even more senior than that).
As expected given the average experience at these firms, Citi and BofA employ the most bankers in New York with over 20 years of experience. Around 18% of each bank’s workforce constitutes of professionals with more than 20 years of experience.
Goldman and Morgan Stanley were the other extreme, with just around 12.5% of their workforce constituting these professionals. The difference is significant; it suggests that each MD at Citi or BofA has 4 people working for them, and each MD at Goldman or Morgan Stanley has around 7 people working for them.
The New York figures are pretty similar to what’s seen in Europe. At Deutsche Bank </news/deutsche-bank-has-been-cutting-junior-staff-in-london-adding-managing-directors> in London, for example, the median seniority is “Vice President”, and the vast majority of its staff are either VPs, AVPs, or directors.

item.title: Boutique bank PWP had a decent 2025 in London. Pay fell drastically
item.description:
Boutique investment bank </news/boutique-investment-banks> Perella Weinberg Partners (PW) did not have a very good 2025 </news/boutique-investment-banks> globally. Revenue fell by 14%, and the firm’s compensation fell by 32%. But what about in London?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Full year 2025 figures for the firm’s UK subsidiary, Perella Weinberg UK Limited – which were published today – suggest an answer: PWP’s London office did great. Mostly. Advisory fee income increased by 30%, reaching £77m ($102m), but total revenue decreased slightly – from £119m ($160m) to £118m ($157m).
Why? Well, because “related party income” fell by 32%. This is because PWP re-allocated profit and loss globally, and even with London performing well, “profits and losses have been allocated such that each affiliate earns the same operating margin,” the firm’s accounts explained.
PWP’s Londoners, despite their success, suffered. The firm paid an average of £339k ($454k) in 2025, which was 31% down on the £490k ($657k) it paid on average in 2024. That’s basically on par with what happened globally.
For what it’s worth, it’s not like PWP’s Londoners took the brunt of the global pain. The highest-paid director at PWP – very likely Dietrich Becker, the firm’s president – had his or her pay cut from £24m ($32m) to £5m ($7.2m), a 78% decrease. Ouch.
The only real upside is that the firm increased hiring in 2025 – from 161 people to 170. The increase was driven by an increase in advisory professionals, 10 of them to be exact, and a decrease in “administration” employees.
It’s not entirely clear how many of those new 2025 faces are still there now. It was announced in May this year that PWP was planning to cut </news/pwp-cuts-tim-shacklock> 10% of its workforce, which would be around 17 people in London. It’s also not clear how those cuts will mix with PWP’s acquisition of Gleacher Shacklock, its 28 people, and especially the presence of Tim Shacklock, formerly London’s highest paid banker.

item.title: Optiver raised pay to £592k in London but its people elsewhere earned more
item.description:
2025 was a bumper year for electronic trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>, and many of the major players raised compensation </news/how-much-do-electronic-trading-jobs-really-pay> for their traders </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> as a result. Accounts for Optiver's UK entities suggest that they're no exception, but payrises at the Dutch firm don't look as extravagant as those seen at Jane Street.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*7vm9lb*_gcl_au*MTExMzQ2MjM2Ny4xNzg1MjI0Nzkx>✍️
Optiver released accounts for three entities this week, only one of which, 'Optiver UK Limited,' reported headcount and pay figures. Those accounts showed that the firm had increased its UK headcount from 133 to 148. Optiver UK's spending on compensation ('wages' plus 'profit sharing') had increased to £591.5k ($792k) per head. The overall spending on profit sharing in the entity had increased by 46.6% despite the firm reporting an increase of just 29% for its global profits for the year back in March. Optiver's London traders may therefore be high performers.
Optiver has ten times the amount of London staff it had in 2020. The firm has also doubled its UK headcount since 2022, the year it moved into a new office in the city; Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-06-01/optiver-opens-new-london-office-as-british-hiring-spree-ramps-up> reported at the time that the new office had enough space for 200 employees, so there's presumably plenty of room for more.
Optiver pays staff in its other offices more. Accounts filed for the firm's Australian entity in May <https://www.afr.com/companies/financial-services/optiver-australia-staff-paid-1-4m-on-average-as-profits-surge-20260512-p5zvx2> showed that Optiver paid 443 employees an average of AUD1.4m ($996.2k). Average pay in the UK isn't that much more than the $700k packages that Optiver is giving to its 2027 graduate hires. </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street>

item.title: Balyasny Asset Management paid its average UK portfolio manager £1.5m last year. But do not be deceived
item.description:
It's filing season for UK hedge funds and trading firms. The flurry of accounts filed for 2025 include a series for Balyasny Asset Management (BAM), the large multistrategy hedge fund run by the friendly figure of Dmitry Balyasny.
BAM files accounts for three UK entities: the partnership (Balyasny Asset Management LLP) and two support subsidiaries (Balyasny International Ltd and Balyasny International II Ltd).
Across each of these three entities, BAM employed 502 people last year. This was 62 people more than in 2024. How much you get paid at the hedge fund in London will depend upon which entity you work for.
Balyasny Asset Management LLP houses the portfolio managers and investment staff. Here, pay averaged £1.53m last year (up from £1.46m in 2024.
Balyasny International Ltd houses some undefined support staff. Here, pay averaged £334k last year (up from £291k in 2024).
Balyasny International II Ltd houses some more undefined support staff. Here, pay fell to £320k last year, (down from £329k in 2024).
325 people work in the support entities. The rest are portfolio managers and investment staff. Last year, Balyasny's UK entities hired 16 new portfolio managers and analysts and 46 new support staff
There is more to life in a hedge fund than wages and salaries. Balyasny Asset Management LLP) also generated £35m in profits to be distributed between members (partners), and one partner received nearly the whole lot. However, that partner was not a human but another entity, Balyasny International Asset Management Limited. This employs the same people as the partnership. Nearly the entire £35m was reinvested in this company, with around £9m disappearing for a likely tax charge.
Unusually, BAM advises people combing through its accounts not to be deceived by average pay figures. It says they are skewed by "portfolio managers with strong performance in the year." This applies to support staff too.

item.title: Qube Research and Technologies has been hiring heavily, paying less
item.description:
Quantitative hedge fund Qube Research and Technologies likes to hire people. But the more it hires, the less it seems to pay.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Newly filed accounts for Qube Research and Technologies Ltd. show that in the year ending December 2025, Qube increased its global headcount 62% to 1,336 people, up from 827 the previous year. Over the same period, average pay per head fell from £722k ($967k) to £616k.
It might be that Qube has become more parsimonious as it's grown. Or it might just be that the new hires are increasingly in low cost countries outside the UK. Qube now has offices in London, Paris, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Denmark and Mumbai. The UK still accounts for 62% of Qube's headcount, but the Mumbai office (and maybe something in Poland </news/fast-growing-quant-fund-building-new-team-in-low-cost-tech-hub>) are likely to pull pay down.
Qube doesn't have partners. It does have directors, whom it is paying more than before. Last year, its highest paid director earned £3.7m, up from £2.4m in '24. If you're a Qube director and it likes you, it might also give you a loan. Three years ago, a director there received a loan of £1.25m, repayable with interest. By last December, he of she had paid £833k of it back.
Qube made £2.9bn in revenues last year, up from £2.3bn in 2024. Net profits went from £712m to £831m over the period.
Qube also paid £499m in interim dividends last year, up from £362m in 2024. These were seemingly distributed as profits were earned. It's not entirely clear who received them as Qube is owned by Guernesy-based 1751 Capital Holding Ltd. However, chief executive Pierre-Yves Morlat and directors Laurent Laizet, Christina Wilgress, Stuart Brown and Marcus Knight are presumably not badly off.
As we reported last week, Qube is diversifying beyond its historic systematic focus. It already has a discretionary equities team and is now building an - allegedly large </news/fast-growing-quant-fund-building-new-team-in-low-cost-tech-hub> - discretionary macro team too.
