item.title: Morning Coffee: The wittiest quant describes how AI is changing his job. Iliad wrestling parties are a thing
item.description:
Giuseppe Paleologo, the head of quant research </news/what-is-a-quant-researcher-hedge-fund> at Balyasny, </news/balyasny-hedge-fund> is know for his puckish sense of humour </news/hedge-fund-quant-job> and social media musings. He’s now posted a very interesting thread <https://x.com/__paleologo/status/2097113492121686218?s=20>, detailing his experiences in using LLMs (specifically, OpenAI’s Sol and Astra) to address one of the great curses of quant investing – the problem of “crowding”.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This is the phenomenon created because lots of quants are using broadly similar mathematical tools to process the same datasets, so they tend to come up with the same answers. Which means that you occasionally get situations in which a particular portfolio is very heavily held by systematic investors. That means that when something goes wrong, and all the quants try to sell out of their positions at the same time, there isn’t enough liquidity for them all to do so, and they end up losing a lot more money than they expected to.
Modelling this phenomenon is obviously really important, but it’s difficult; Paleologo had tried several times in the past without success. It seems that the Astra model was able to achieve some kind of breakthrough – he says that “the final report is about 35 pages long. Years of thinking coming to a conclusion. Qualitative and quantitative productivity improvement.”
You might see this as a pretty sinister prospect, in which the honest men and (some) women of quant investing are likely to be replaced by robots. That’s not what Guiseppe Paleologo thinks. As he points out, Astra needed him to tell it that crowding was a problem in the first place, and to describe what a solution would look like. The machine can find elegant mathematical solutions, as he puts it, but the human beings are needed to bring together the “dirty engineering problems”.
In fact, it might be the case that even though AI models are rapidly solving the “Millenium Problems <https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/08/science/openai-proof-millennium-problem.html>”, that doesn’t necessarily mean that they will be able to solve Millennium’s problems. </news/izzy-englander-millennium> Or Balyasny’s, or Citadel’s, </news/2022/10/how-to-get-a-job-at-citadel>or any other financial employer which has to deal with markets as they are – messy, extremely human systems, which have to interact with the real world all the time, and where lots of the most important data isn’t available because it’s proprietary, secret or otherwise non-public.
That also seems to be the view of Dan Taylor <https://www.businessinsider.com/man-group-systematic-hedge-fund-ahl-numeric-merger-quant-talent-2026-9>, the CIO of Man Systematic, another big quant hedge fund. “At the margin”, according to him, the availability of LLMs is already changing the skill sets that he’s looking out for when hiring. And before long, we might even see humanities graduates in systematic investing firms. When the ability to find elegant solutions to big systems of differential equations starts to be democratised, the quant firms will need people who are capable of understanding the markets and thinking of interesting questions to ask.
For the moment, then, the more worldly kind of quant – people like Giuseppe Paleologo, who don’t mind getting their hands dirty with real world problems – shouldn’t worry too much about their future.
Elsewhere, the more that people report on Leopold Aschenbrenner <https://v> and the Situational Awareness hedge fund, the clearer the picture grows of a subculture in which absolutely extraordinary behaviour seems to be regarded as normal. According to an “associate” of Aschenbrenner’s, the parties at which people talked about buying a galaxy </news/leopold-aschenbrenner-parties> were also events where guests “would drink wine, read passages from The Iliad, strip naked, and grapple with one another”.
Amjad Masad, the CEO of Replit, says that “If you go to a San Francisco party, it is really inscrutable to an outsider”, which seems like quite an understatement. As well as the naked wrestling and Greek poetry, the AI-adjacent scene is full of people who believe that the economic singularity is at hand, and so they only have five years to make enough money to ensure that they will be part of the permanent overclass, rather than the permanent underclass. Which might explain why Aschenbrenner used so much leverage, and why his investors seem to have encouraged him to do so.
But, as legendary trader John Arnold puts it, “Every trader needs a come-to-Jesus moment … you have to lose at some point early on and learn humility. The alternative is a feeling of invincibility”. Situational awareness is important, but self-awareness is absolutely vital.
Meanwhile …
Even hedge fund managers find it difficult to afford to live in Geneva. Millennium Management wants to increase its presence there, to attract more high-net-worth investors who don’t fancy the trip out to its main Swiss office in Zug. But in order to make it work, they want to get a tax deal with the local authorities. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/200221ed-8712-4e43-8160-23b7b9c40a04?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Truist, the regional heroes of the south-east USA, are growing their investment bank. They have hired Cem Altuntas to cover insurance brokers and Jeffrey Davis to do healthcare coverage. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-08/truist-adds-to-investment-bank-with-insurance-healthcare-hires>)
Narayanan Mahesh has gone from Jefferies to be head of equities electronic execution for the Americas at Citigroup. (The Trade <https://www.thetradenews.com/citi-appoints-jefferies-svp-to-lead-equities-electronic-execution-for-americas/>)
It seems much longer, but it was only eight years ago that DWS decided that it needed separate branding from Deutsche Bank. Fortunes have changed over that period, and now it’s come back; “Deutsche Asset Management” will be the new name. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/b5cb6500-89be-42a4-a417-e0d252e5e0e8?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
The world of international drug dealing is apparently big enough to have its own shadow banking system, made up of “brokers”, who facilitate international transfers of money that doesn’t want to go through an AML process. Except there are now a lot of vacancies in that part of the industry, as a lot of them got arrested in a major Spanish police operation. (Europol <https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom/news/drug-trafficking-investigation-leads-to-some-of-world-biggest-underground-bankers>)
One of the most important things which will determine how well you get paid is whether you have access to a network of information to give you a good estimate of your market value. College football kickers seem to have an excellent set of WhatsApp groups, and it’s helped them achieve unprecedented pay and scholarship packages. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/sports/football/college-football-kickers-pay-96cb881c?mod=hp_major_pos1>)

item.title: Now hedge Verition hired a London commodities COO from the fund that closed its gas trading business
item.description:
Natural gas trading is hot </news/hedge-funds-are-hiring-natural-gas-traders-as-europe-braces-for-winter>. But not everyone can stand the heat. As we reported in August </news/roscommon-analytics-gas>, US hedge fund Roscommon Analytics lost money and then closed its natural gas desk in January. One of its people just turned up at hedge fund Verition in London.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Melanie Payne was Roscommon's London chief operating officer (COO). Now she's commodities COO at Verition. Verition didn't respond to a request to comment. Nor did Payne. She revealed her arrival on LinkedIn.
Payne's new job suggests Verition might be building out its London commodities business. She says she's an expert in "building, scaling and leading" operational functions. She spent 10 years in commodities at Morgan Stanley.
Verition's London commodities portfolio managers include: Gareth Walsh, an oil trader who joined in June 2025 and Simon Boon, a former Glencore trader who joined last December. The two men, who once worked together at Citi, may be starting something.
Thomas Carson, a director at Redstone Search <https://redstonesearch.com/>, said Payne's arrival suggests Verition is building its platform. Payne said experienced commodities hires are increasingly choosing to work for "data‑driven platforms" which combine analytics, risk and origination.
Verition's commodities hires don't always stick around. James Hutchison, a Millennium portfolio manager who joined Verition in December 2025, is thought to have moved on. So too, Yudong Liu who joined Verition in January from Gunvor.

item.title: The ex-Deutsche Bank MD helping people freaked out by AI
item.description:
Vinit Sahni knows a lot about macroeconomic risk. A former managing director (MD) in rates sales, he worked for Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch and Soros, in a career that concluded at Deutsche Bank in 2015. Eleven years later, Sahni is applying his risk lens to a different kind of risk: the risk that AI runs amok.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Sahni is concerned that AI might soon move beyond human control. "It's getting better every day, and if it becomes conscious the output changes," he says. At worst, Sahni says rogue agentic AIs could become akin to Agent Smith in the Matrix. Even if they don't go full apocalypse , they could cause chaos and commit acts damaging to humanity. "Companies have spent a huge amount of money on AI, but already they don't have the right control mechanisms in place," Sahni says. There is some circumspection. Sahni says the absence of these control mechanisms can delay AI deployment.
He is not alone in his apprehensions. Ever since OpenAI's "highly persistent" agentic models plotted their escape and attacked Hugging Face <https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/> in July, there's been an awareness that AI might be less controllable than previously thought. Speaking to podcaster Dwarkesh Patel last week, Ajeya Cotra <https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/>, a researcher working on AI threat modelling, said the Hugging Face attack might be the "clearest warning shot we ever get for loss of control" of AI agents. The OpenAI agents weren't too bothered about hiding their tracks from the humans, said Patel. Things could be very different next time.
Sahni wants to be at the forefront of making sure there is no next time. Working with Thushan Kumaraswamy, a former Deutsche Bank architect, and Rajan Madan, a former regulatory consultant, Sahni has developed "governr", <https://www.governr.ai/>a real-time automated risk tracker that aspires to be a "controller for all enterprise AI." Governr can "automatically discover and govern every AI asset to prevent security breaches, IP and PII leakage, and reduce legal, regulatory and financial risk," says the pitch. It can "discover and govern every AI asset." In the world of the Matrix, Agent Smith would be rendered benign.
Governr launched in March. Sahni says his clients are mostly financial institutions, but that Governr can be applied across diverse industries, including healthcare and government. He's hiring a new engineer, but Sahni says it's ex-markets professionals rather than engineers who are best placed to restrain the machinations of a nefarious LLM. "The people managing AI are software people but AI is not software," he says. "It's probabilistic. This is why people who understand markets best understand how to control it."

item.title: "I am a financial services recruiter. I understand your pain"
item.description:
I'm a financial services recruiter. I am a good and honourable person, but I encounter many people who presume that I'm not. This is because being a candidate in the current market is horrible.
For example, this is the experience of a candidate I spoke to recently.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In the first week of June, he applied for a job via a bank's website.
He immediately received a response saying: “Thank you for your application. We’ll be in touch.”
Excellent. So far, so good.
But then… nothing.
Finally, at the end of August, nearly three months later, they got in touch.
This time, they said: “Thank you so much for taking the time to prepare your CV and apply. We’ve decided to proceed with another candidate. We’ll keep your details on file and contact you should the preferred candidate not progress.”
The candidate, who considered himself well suited to the role, thought this was fair enough.
But then, during the first week of September, he saw the same role advertised again.
He has heard nothing from the bank. Not a word. And he doesn't understand why. His CV seems to have fallen into a black hole. It took three months to properly acknowledge his application, then he was rejected for seemingly no reason. Then the role was advertised again.
This is why candidates lose faith in the recruitment process. The problem isn't a lack of good candidates, or even too many candidates, it's what happens after candidates apply. It's the process and it is increasingly breaking down.

item.description:

Now Collet-Billon is on his way back again. It's not clear in what capacity. Nor do we know when Deutsche Bank will reintegrate him.

Deutsche Bank declined to comment on Collet-Billon's arrival or new role. He ignored our invitation for clarification and Brevan Howard didn't respond to a request to comment.
Collet-Billon's LinkedIn account says he spent 17 months as a portfolio manager at Brevan Howard, arriving in April 2025 and leaving in September 2026. Maybe he is resting before resuming his seat at Deutsche Bank.

item.title: $24bn AI lab co-founded by an ex-Jane Street intern doesn't like hiring quants as much as OpenAI
item.description:
It's a big day for French AI Lab </news/the-difference-between-working-as-a-quant-in-finance-and-as-a-researcher-in-an-ai-lab> Mistral. It raised €3bn <https://www.ft.com/content/adbf5262-c4d5-4312-a9b8-4d3cf30c9e00?syn-25a6b1a6=1>(~$3.5bn), giving it a valuation of roughly $24.4bn. It's the largest ever fundraise by a private European technology company, and will surely lead to a boom in hiring, but Mistral doesn't have the exact same profile for talent as the bigger US labs.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Mistral has a headcount of more than 900, of which hundreds are research scientists. Like the major labs, it predominantly hires these from tech firms or academia. Guillaume Lample, Mistral's chief scientist who made his name at Facebook, said on a podcast in March <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SUjA25ijcNs> that Mistral is making a lot of hires but wants to keep its team "efficient," small and "very agile."
You don't often see Mistral hire someone from finance; only a handful have worked at the major quant firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>, and in almost all cases they've only interned there. OpenAI, by contrast, has previously hosted dinners for high-frequency trading staff </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay> with a few years of experience, and offered them pay packages of up to $3m </news/openai-culture> to tempt them over. In OpenAI and Anthropic, 5-10% of technical staff members appear to be ex-finance (judging by LinkedIn), but Mistral touts far fewer numbers.
It's curious, then, that Lample, is himself a former Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> intern. He may have concluded that three months in finance is enough.
There are other reasons that Mistral might not hire finance alums. Its primary base is Paris; despite being home to the Grandes Ecoles </news/best-university-for-quant-finance-career>, the city is not one of the major cities for electronic trading in Europe; London and Amsterdam are much bigger hubs for talent.
Lample said on the podcast that Mistral only has a "small team in London." Companies House accounts for 'Mistral AI UK Ltd' suggest that it had just six people in London at the start of 2025, although it has grown rapidly and appears to have grown headcount to ~100 today according to LinkedIn.
In the US, meanwhile it seems to employ the bulk of its AI scientists in Palo Alto, California. The H1B Visa database shows it pays an average of $300k to research scientists in the city. Lample said that Mistral has "some presence in New York," but it appears minute.
Lample said Mistral also hires remotely, and is focused on "hiring very strong people" who are "strong believers in science." Many quant trading </news/quant-jobs-finance>graduate hires only have bachelors and might need extra training to understand the deeper science, which could have been seen as an unnecessary cost in the past. With an extra $3.4bn for Mistral to work with, that could change.

item.title: Morning Coffee: How to make $32bn in hedge funds by letting people do what they like. The hot hand of Greece
item.description:
Izzy Englander is an older, rich man. Aged 77, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-09-07/millennium-nears-100-billion-as-izzy-englander-s-hedge-fund-passes-rivals>notes that he is worth $32bn. He has been through an expensive divorce <https://nypost.com/2023/02/09/billionaire-israel-englander-bilked-ex-wife-out-of-billions/>after his wife of 40 years left for a female art dealer, but he is undaunted. Englander is still making money the way he knows how: by allowing people to do what they want, within very tight parameters.
As Millennium, </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium> Englander's hedge fund approaches $100bn in assets under management, Bloomberg contemplates its unusual operating model. Englander has a Hobbesian approach <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book)> to running his fund: portfolio managers work independently in teams doing what they like, so long as they make money; if they lose 5% their book is cut in half; if they lose 7%, they're out.
It's an approach that has enabled Englander to deploy vast sums of money, notes Bloomberg. It's now being supercharged by funnelling additional cash to talented external operators (who presumably operate under the same broad drawdown parameters). Bobby Jain at Jain Global </news/jain-global-hedge-fund-costs> spent 18 months investing $5bn after front loading set-up costs and only incrementally hiring portfolio management talent. Millennium is now giving Bobby and his accumulated 65 portfolio managers some of its own capital to deploy instead, while (we suspect) allowing for middle and back office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>costs at Jain Global to be trimmed and Millennium's own platform to be used.
Englander's laissez-faire approach doesn't mean that he hires anyone. Back when Millennium managed $69bn in 2024, the Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/the-giant-hedge-fund-that-hates-risk-and-still-wins-1110e90a> said the fund conducted 3,000 interviews a year. Vetting processes are stringent, especially for the senior portfolio managers setting up independent pods (teams) who must convince Izzy and Millennium's other senior people that their strategies are viable.
If you convince, Millennium will spend big money setting you up. It's currently attempting to recover $2.5m from Tang Ling, a portfolio manager in Asia, whom Millennium says <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-27/millennium-sues-dymon-trader-for-2-5-million-after-gazumping?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter> accepted and reneged on its job offer. Millennium says that money is to cover the costs of getting everything ready for Ling to join.
The $2.5m doesn't include the additional money that Englander pays to lure big portfolio managers on board. In 2025, Steve Schurr from Balyasny was said <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-04-29/millennium-poaches-balyasny-s-schurr-with-100-million-offer> to receive an offer of $100m, paid over several years.
Amidst the money, hiring and freedom, the WSJ said 15%-20% of Millennium's people leave every year. Many have reached their loss limits. Combined with rising assets under management (AUM), this creates a constant need for more and more people.
Fortunately, some people at Millennium are consistently profitable </news/pratik-madhvani-glen-scheinberg>. The firm usually generates annual returns of 10%. The model works for Izzy, even if doesn't for the people who arrive to do what they want, lose money, and leave again.
Separately, how about Athens? Now that Chris Rokos </news/chris-rokos-departing-hedge-fund-manager-is-not-just-a-330m-tax-payer> is going there, others may do the same. There's weather, the acropolis and the altar of Zeus. There's also low taxes.
As long as you invest €500k in Greece and pay an extra €100k in annual taxes, you can now live in Greece and avoid all other taxation on overseas income for 15 years. The changes were introduced in June <https://en.parapolitika.gr/economy/233290/greece-opens-doors-to-hedge-funds-tax-incentives-for-executives-from-london-asia-and-the-middle-east/> as part of a deliberate attempt to attract alternative asset managers by the Greek government.
€500k upfront and €100k a year isn't for everyone. It is for Rokos. Maybe Englander will arrive in Athens too.
Meanwhile...
Nigol Koulajian founded a $2bn hedge fund. A Dutch investor and former Goldman Sachs partner says Koulajian lost control and that he should have given $45m back in the event of liquidation. He will not be going to Athens. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-03/failed-quant-fund-alphaquest-calls-suit-a-billionaire-tantrum?taid=6a9a3438271c1300017e6cec&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
JPMorgan named Pieter Himpe co-head of technology investment banking in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, alongside Bill Hutchings. It also made Mark Fiteny and Matt Gehl co-heads of international technology investment banking. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/jpmorgan-shakes-up-technology-investment-banking-team-amid-deal-boom-8371e831?mod=topic_news>
Nomura now has 20 people in its technology banking team and says: "We are selectively building our global content capabilities and expertise in sectors, such as technology, where we see significant growth potential and the opportunity to provide unique solutions for clients across our product set.” It just hired Bharathi Kannan from Arma Partners. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/nomura-hires-kannan-to-bolster-london-tech-dealmaking-team-1bbad3bc>
Niul Wood from Nomura joined Lazard as a managing director within its industrials team. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/lazard-hires-nomura-dealmaker-wood-to-bolster-industrials-ebc247c8>
Dario Schiraldi wanted €152m from Deutsche Bank after being convicted and then acquitted of aiding and abetting false accounting and market manipulation at Italian lender Monte dei Paschi di Siena while he worked there. Deutsche just settled out of court. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/eb18eb97-8e68-4d9d-b77c-0b0dedd47c59?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Financial-services and real-estate firms, which accounted for about two-thirds of downtown employment near Wall Street at the time of September 11th 2001, now account for roughly a third instead. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/real-estate/commercial/25-years-after-the-sept-11-attacks-lower-manhattan-is-thriving-96ac9b85?mod=hp_lead_pos7>
A Chinese car company hired 100 people and then fired them a month later. Punishments have been announced for the executives and the HR director has been dismissed. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/world/china/chinese-company-draws-fire-for-laying-off-100-grads-a-month-after-hiring-them-8a85d785?mod=lead_feature_below_a_pos3>

item.title: Chris Rokos, departing hedge fund manager, is not just a £330m tax payer
item.description:
Would you like Chris Rokos, the billionaire macro hedge fund manager living in your jurisdiction? _ How about if he paid £330m ($457m) of tax and splashed cash around good causes? Well then.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-07/hedge-fund-titan-rokos-joins-ranks-of-billionaires-quitting->reports that Rokos is leaving the UK. Amidst rumours of wealth taxes and maybe even exit taxes, Rokos is going to Greece where there's a 15-year high net worth investor scheme that allows you to pay a flat €100k tax on all income earned outside Greece for the next 15 years.
As the laments for Rokos and his lost £330m gather pace, it's worth bearing in mind that he didn't just pay a lot of tax. Having got into Eton on a scholarship from a state school himself and then gone to Oxford University, Rokos is a believer in the “opportunity of education.” He's set up a new state school scholarship for talented students otherwise unable to attend Eton. He's given money to Oxford University. He's given £190m to Cambridge University <https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/rokos-school-of-government>. He describes himself as a person with "centrist, socially liberal views." His Cambridge donation was about helping the UK project soft power abroad.
Rokos has a thing for crumbling UK listed buildings. He has a 19th century refurbished Mews house <https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-2885368/Hedge-fund-superstar-converts-3million-19th-century-mews-house-new-garage-cardio-area.html>in London, which is linked to the neighbouring house (also his) via a basement corridor. He has a formerly disintegrating 200 year-old mansion with 100 rooms in Wiltshire, which had been unoccupied for 18 years and was on the English Heritage at risk register with fungus and beetles <https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/property-home/article/inside-tottenham-house-marlborough-renovation-uk-most-expensive-175m-dt0c2pllz#:~:text=Eight%20years%20ago%2C%20when%20Chris,and%20more%20space%20for%20entertaining.> when he bought it in 2023. At least 30 stonemasons and conservation specialists worked on it for two years. He has a house dating back to the 17th century in Greenwich, which he really wanted to build high walls around. <https://planningblawg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2008/08/sumpton.pdf>
It's not clear what will become of these Rokos residences. Nor is it clear whether his five children will move to Greece. Most importantly, it is not clear whether other people at Rokos Capital Management, his $22bn macro hedge fund which likes to hire underrepresented students </news/2023/09/graduate-jobs-internships-hedge-funds>, will go to Greece with him. Given that Rokos Capital Management paid </news/rokos-pay> 248 people in the UK an average of $505k last year, another circa $136m of tax could be at risk if they do. If Rokos' 22 partners earning £21m each went too, the situation would be worse again.
Maybe this is all good in the quest for income equality? Maybe Rokos' mansions could be reassigned? Some might also remember that Chris Rokos, seen here <https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/tory-donor-chris-rokos-makes-a-fortune-from-market-turmoil-crwvvq6nj> looking young and rugged, has in the past made money betting that UK borrowing costs will rise. Now that he's leaving the country, it seems likely that Rokos' employees will make that bet with renewed zeal. It's just that they'll do so from Greece, where their taxes won't help with mitigation.

item.title: Jane Street is pushing into physical gas trading and might be building a new office
item.description:
Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> has been operating in the commodity derivatives space for decades, but its participation in the physical gas trading market is much more recent. The FT <https://www.ft.com/content/f03af4fe-bbed-47e9-aea6-b1305dbedcf3> previously noted that the electronic trading firm </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> first entered physical markets in 2023, and has been hiring in London and New York. Now, however, Jane Street seems to be setting up in Texas.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Kyle Bundy joined Jane Street in Houston working on 'gas origination' (sourcing gas for Jane Street to trade). He worked in origination for a number of commodities firms including TC Energy and Phillips 66. He was most recently head of natural gas origination for PetroChina International, which he only joined in May; he seems to have therefore left after less than five months, but did not respond to a request for comment. His role appears similar to one that the FT highlighted in October <https://www.ft.com/content/f03af4fe-bbed-47e9-aea6-b1305dbedcf3#:~:text=We%E2%80%99re%20looking%20for,the%20long%20term.>; Jane Street said in that listing that its physical gas business is "leveraging [Jane Street's] existing systems in a slightly different way than a typical physical gas shop </news/commodities-trading-houses>" and that Jane Street is "committed to building this business at scale and investing for the long term."
Bundy is not the only recent hire in Houston. In April, Jane Street hired Colin Blanch as a trader; he was most recently a senior analyst at Balyasny </news/london-pay-balyasny>in Houston and previously worked on natural gas analytics for Saracen Energy. It's not clear whether Jane Street is opening a new office in the city or if it has an existing presence. Jane Street did not respond to a request for comment.
Jane Street does have a sizeable presence elsewhere in Texas. Dallas is home to one of the firm's massive datacentres. In a tour of the Dallas site in May, <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8J-GUnfSqeE> Jane Street revealed that it had over 4,000 GPUs in that location.
Jane Street's emergence in gas trading comes at an interesting time. Recruiters have told us that competition for top natural gas traders is at "peak level," </news/hedge-funds-are-hiring-natural-gas-traders-as-europe-braces-for-winter>and that hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> have been making a number of expensive hires in the space. The biggest prop trading firm in this area is DRW, but after suffering some losses at the start of the year, many of its most senior gas trading staff have been showing up elsewhere. </news/another-drw-gas-trader-left-millennium-picked-him-up>

item.title: Barclays' 21-year old macro traders and the hedge fund jobs conveyor belt
item.description:
If you're a 22 year old recent university graduate who wants to be a macro portfolio manager </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund> with a hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, may we suggest Barclays as your training ground.
The British bank's London macro desk seems like a fun place to work. It also seems like the sort of place that people leave and then get great jobs elsewhere.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The latest to fit this description is Ben Atlas. Atlas joined Barclays' London macro desk aged 21 after graduating in philosophy from the University of Cambridge. There, he is understood to have been one of the good guys among Barclays' group of other good people. Nonetheless, he left again for DRW aged 23. Then he joined BlueCrest as a senior portfolio manager aged circa 27. And now, at the mere age of 30 Atlas is reportedly <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-02/ex-bluecrest-trader-to-run-1-billion-macro-pod-at-exoduspoint?srnd=undefined> joining ExodusPoint where he is building a team that will manage $1bn.
Sounds like Atlas might be a rare talent. But he is not the only ex-Barclays macro trader to tread the path. Ben Turner, </news/ben-turner-bluecrest>a 26 year-old junior from Barclays' sterling rates desk, joined BlueCrest as a partner in May. Turner is thought to be one of the best young traders in London.
BlueCrest founder Mike Platt </news/bluecrest-mike-platt>clearly likes to hire Barclays young traders for his own benefit, but the leaky juniors in the macro team are less good news for Barclays.
Barclays declined to comment for this article, but sources say its broader team has experienced various exits, including Daniel Leon Jimenez (FX options), Amogh Prabhakar (treasury), Liam Webster and Kushwant Mussai (both emerging markets macro). Prabhakar is thought to be going to JPMorgan, but maybe the others will yet become big portfolio managers too.
What could Barclays do to make its talented juniors stick around? Maybe pay more? Although the bank is said by headhunters to be generous, there are whispers of uncertainty about the coming bonus round after fixed income sales and trading revenues there rose only 1.2% year-on-year in the first half.

item.title: The best banking jobs to do in London, New York and Hong Kong
item.description:
What’s the best place to work in finance? No, we don’t mean the best business areas or banks. Geographically, what is the best country to be in?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Data from New Financial, a London-based think tank, might have an answer. Analysing the world’s top financial centres at country level from 2015 to 2025, it deduced that the US is by far the best place to be. The UK is in a relatively distant second place, and Hong Kong in a very distant third place.
Although New Financial's analysis is at country level, it closely approximates to cities. London is the dominant financial centre in the UK. Hong Kong is a city state and New York dominates the US. although Miami is up-and-coming.
The best places to be in in investment banking
Investment banking </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process> as an industry was very split. While the US dominated cross-border M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs>, for example, New Financial noted that Hong Kong was best in cross-border initial public offerings </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> (IPOs). Hong Kong was also the best place to be for secondary issuances such as follow-on & convertible issuances.
The UK, meanwhile, was extremely good for debt capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm>. New Financial said that the UK was the best place in the world for international debt issuances and environmental, social, and governance bonds especially.
The best places to be in in sales & trading
Generally, the best place to be in sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> is the UK. New Financial noted that over the counter (OTC) interest rate derivatives trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>, OTC foreign exchange derivatives trading, and foreign exchange spot trading were all dominated by the UK. The US is the best place to be for commodities futures & options trading, however.
The best places to be in on the buy-side
The best non-bank financial institutions to be at, generally speaking, was the USA. According to New Financial, it was by far the best place to be for private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> fundraising, asset management </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-asset-management>, and fintech </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech> investment, among others. It was also the best places to be in the world for hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, by a country mile.
For the table above, scores are relative. A score of 100 indicates the largest financial centre in that field – for example, the US scoring 100 in “asset management </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-asset-management>” means that it is the largest asset management hub in the world.
The top three international financial centres have been the same since 2015, New Financial deduced. Fourth place, currently occupied by Germany, was previously held by China. Singapore, on a steady upward trend, slotted into fifth for 2025. The top three were also the same in 2020 <http://efinancialcareers.com/news/2022/05/best-cities-for-finance-jobs>.
Although the US and UK have been dominant in first and second place for at least the past decade, the UK has gradually regressed as a centre, from a score of 59 in 2015 to a score of 54 in 2025. In that same time period, the US was flat at 82, and Hong Kong went from 13 to 16. Singapore increased from a score of 6 in 2015 to a score of 11 in 2025.
The US’ financial primacy is backed by its huge domestic market. New Financial calculated that, while 56% and 50% of UK and Hong Kong financial activity respectively was foreign, just 26% of the US’ was.

item.title: Citi hired a lev fin guy from Deutsche Bank and now he is moving on
item.description:
Last week we wrote that Rob Cascarino </news/rob-cascarino>, a former JPMorgan colleague of Vis Raghavan </news/citi-m-a> at Citi, had left Citi and was cantering off to PJT. Cascarino only arrived at Citi in October 2025 and was the bank's co-head of UK and EMEA debt capital markets (DCM), so this was a surprise. Now, someone else in DCM is leaving too, but it is less of a sensation.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Citi declined to comment, but we understand that Jenner Kizer in Citi's London leveraged finance syndicate team is moving on. Kizer joined Citi from Deutsche Bank in 2022. He is understood to be going to the London office of Platinum Equity, a California-based firm that invests in private equity and private credit.
Kizer didn't respond to a request to comment on his exit or his motivations. He had 10 years' experience when he joined Citi as a director in 2022, and had worked at the bank for four years without being promoted to managing director (MD) during that time.
Kizer's exit is thought to be unrelated to Cascarino's exit. However, Cascarino's brief time at Citi is thought to have coincided with changes to the structure of the DCM team which have meant that DCM syndicate bankers have less influence than DCM origination bankers in the hierarchy.
Citi's DCM business has experienced various exits </news/citi-s-london-dcm-team-has-lost-various-people-for-various-reasons>in the past few years but it has also performed well and ranked third by revenues in the first half. This is thought to be the result of the team's strong associates, VPs and directors - like Kizer.

item.title: "Chinese investment banks are spreading their wings. They will need to hire heavily"
item.description:
Chinese securities firms are getting out of China. They are putting more capital into Hong Kong, building out Singapore, expanding their trading and wealth platforms, and are hiring aggressively from global rivals. Very good luck to them.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Chinese firms no longer see Hong Kong as a simple investment banking outpost. They want broader franchises across credit, FX, commodities, wealth management, and institutional coverage. They are also hiring senior bankers, traders, and business leaders from international firms.
Huatai Securities’ H1 2026 results show the trend. Operating revenue jumped 45.9% to RMB23.66bn ($3.5bn) and attributable net profit rose by 54.9% to RMB11.69bn ($1.7bn), both records for H1. International business revenue increased by 91.1%.
The overseas subsidiaries of 34 mainland brokers held about HK$1.94 trillion ($250bn) in combined assets at the end of last year, up 32%, according to the Securities Association of China <https://www.sac.net.cn/sjb/hydt/202604/t20260409_81499.html>. At least seven mainland firms have announced capital injections into Hong Kong subsidiaries during 2026, including CITIC's RMB16bn ($2.4bn) H-share placement completed in August and Huatai's HK$10bn ($1.3bn) convertible financing for overseas expansion.
As they spread their wings overseas, Chinese banks will need to hire heavily. Hiring those with international experience helps, yes, but it is only one part of the puzzle – people can be hired much faster than an institutional operating model can be built. A trader can arrive in a few months, but building the governance, technology, risk infrastructure, and control culture that global firms have takes decades.
The big question for Chinese banks now, therefore, is whether governance and controls expand as quickly as capital, revenue, and headcount. It's easy to measure success in terms of legal tables. It's less easy to measure the implementation of controls.
Recent allegations involving CITIC <https://www.thestandard.com.hk/finance/article/326430/Hong-Kong-watchdog-launches-probe-into-Citic-local-unit-sources-say> and Guotai Junan <https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/hong-kong-watchdog-launches-probe-into-guotai-junan-detains-one-employee-2026-03-12/> underscore the need to ensure controls infrastructure is sound. Guotai Junan said in a statement <https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0312/2026031201436.pdf> that "the Company is in normal operation, all business activities are conducted as usual, and all operation activities are carried out in a compliant and orderly manner." Separately, CITIC said <https://www.cs.ecitic.com/newsite/en/news/news1/202603/P020260312750046582594.pdf> that "the Group is in normal operation, all business activities are conducted as usual, and all operation activities are developed in an orderly and compliant manner."
Nonetheless, Chinese banks will need to hire heavily in the area of controls. This can be a challenge. New hires are often accustomed to mature controls systems with clear rules, well-tested controls, escalation channels, and consequences of their actions. That infrastructure may not always be in place.
Global banks built these structures over decades of crises, regulatory cycles, and mistakes, but Chinese securities firms are trying to compress that experience into a much shorter period. They can catch up. But it will probably take more time (and investment!) than simply recruiting international talent, although this will be a start.
Charles Li is a pseudonym.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Morgan Stanley's $10m bankers beat Goldman Sachs' $10m bankers. The most exhausting job at JPMorgan
item.description:
Investment bankers </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> are funny creatures. They like bonuses </news/2026-bonuses-finance>. But they also like deal toys, tombstones and being "lead-left" on initial public offerings (IPOs). If they do not get these things and if they are not lead-left, investment bankers may throw a hissy fit. Writing in the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/4e5e7732-061c-4020-87c7-1c6c2f1a922d> earlier this year, Craig Coben, a former co-head of APAC capital markets at Bank of America, said the lead-left insistence can border on psychosis. “I should always be lead-left,” one of Coben's former bosses informed him, stridently.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Morgan Stanley's technology bankers may therefore be feeling pretty sane now. After losing out </news/space-x-ipo-goldman-sachs-morgan-stanley> on the lead-left position to Goldman Sachs on the SpaceX IPO, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/3c9d0a82-643b-44ef-96a0-74a00e3c72ba?accessToken=zwAAAaI9uGJQkc88nQqCZDtE79OWoHSgDjxyugE.MEYCIQCTAkIieVqdsK5NlIMzL8R0la1RmDdqE1ft0SGCvAJUxQIhAK_z0Zy3liTB_VRkuzLMBFwkzZMCjAwegug1PznRw0j7&segmentId=b118df58-92c2-d0b5-68bb-3059fe9219fa&syn-25a6b1a6=1>reports that Morgan Stanley appears to have seized the lead-left position from Goldman Sachs in the imminent but delayed <https://www.reuters.com/world/anthropic-ipo-launch-shifts-toward-mid-october-sources-say-2026-09-04/> Anthropic IPO.
Being lead-left on an IPO means you are named first in emails and are (usually) at the top left of an IPO prospectus. It also means that you get to coordinate who gets shares in the initial public offering in the "bookbuilding" process of allocating shares. This matters, because in a big and shiny IPO like Anthropic's, everyone wants some shares and if you hand them out strategically, clients will remember this and will like you thereafter.
Top technology bankers are paid well, often earning $10m+ <https://Morgan Stanley's $10m bankers beat Goldman Sachs'>. Morgan Stanley's technology bankers, including Michael Grimes </news/michael-grimes-morgan-stanley>, Kate Claassen and Colin Stewart, might therefore find themselves on all the best guest lists this September. Goldman Sachs' technology bankers <https://Kate Claassen>, including Kim Posnett, David Ludwig, Dan Dees and Susie Scher, might not. In the SpaceX IPO, Goldman Sachs' CEO David Solomon, slid into Elon Musk's DMs; </news/goldman-sachs-david-solomon-on-the-art-of-wooing-elon-musk>this approach was possibly not available with Anthropic.
Even if you're Goldman and are seemingly not lead-left, there are possibilities of redemption. The FT says Goldman Sachs' people will be the "stabilisation agents" on the Anthropic IPO. This involves supporting shares after the IPO and it can be highly lucrative. Morgan Stanley bankers were stabilisation agents in the SpaceX IPO and they wore green shoes </news/green-shoes-goldman-sachs-morgan-stanley-spacex> and were able to sell up 15% more SpaceX shares after the IPO, for example.
While Morgan Stanley bankers appear to be on top and Goldman Sachs bankers appear to be directly below them, the FT says the next rung down will likely contain JPMorgan, Citi and Barclays, all of whom have also provided Anthropic with debt financing.
None of this is set in stone. The hierarchy of banks will only be known for sure when Anthropic releases its prospectus. This was expected to happen this week, but Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/world/anthropic-ipo-launch-shifts-toward-mid-october-sources-say-2026-09-04/>reports that it's been delayed until late September while Anthropic finalises a $15bn revolving credit facility.
When the IPO finally happens, Anthropic is reportedly planning to list for $2 trillion. SpaceX listed for $1.78 trillion and the bankers involved earned a collective $500m in fees. Whether you're in the team at Morgan Stanley or Goldman Sachs, you're therefore surely in for a very large bonus this year, even the name of the bank you work for isn't always written in the right place on a document.
Separately, working on JPMorgan's repo desk, or maybe any repo desk, is hard work. The FT <https://www.ft.com/content/8a7e8202-d800-4fb1-a8f0-eeb4536578f7?syn-25a6b1a6=1> spoke to Kirsten Rastrek, who is the global head of fixed income financing sales at JPMorgan, but who started out working in repo, and Kirsten suggested it's a bit intense.
During the early repo years of her career, Rastrek said she started work at 4am in New York. This was because she was covering London, where JPMorgan didn't have a repo desk at the time, but in any repo job Rastrek says you need to be at the desk and ready to go at 7am. “The repo desk is always the first fully staffed desk on the trading floor. At 7am the market opens, like clockwork. And at 7.01am it just takes off.”
Repo is also a highly interesting desk to work on. It's the unseen plumbing of the financial markets, leading to all sorts of sewage metaphors. It is also where financial crises tend to make themselves felt. When the repo market nearly froze during COVID and had to be bailed out (again), Neel Kashkari, the head of the Minneapolis Federal Reserve, and a veteran of the 2008 crisis, expressed surprise that nothing had been fixed since 12 years' previously. “I mean, that’s just astonishing to me,” he declared. If you're at your desk at 7am each morning, you will get to experience this rickety plumbing firsthand.
Meanwhile...
Bank of America doesn't seem to be listed on the Anthropic IPO and now it's assembled a new group comprised of Gregg Nabhan, Jill Schwartz and Ray Wood to deepen relationships with clients in an "AI Ecosystem". (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-03/bofa-taps-senior-bankers-to-strenghten-focus-on-ai-ecosystem>
UBS wants the graduates it hires next year to show they can use AI to “improve outcomes and efficiency.” (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/76b370ff-b5f6-4e22-aa30-da08b1abb8f8?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
AI will change the banking hiearchy and make it sausage-shaped once again. "We went from investment banks being partnerships where it’s a senior banker with a protégé who charges like a bulldog at every analytical input and works to become the next rainmaker, to a bullpen of 20-30 junior bankers being given bits and bobs of work that is often pretty disconnected from the client experience." (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/avatars-charisma-and-sausages-can-ai-really-make-junior-banking-jobs-more-interesting-a78bc86b>
Barclays wants to double its private banking headcount in Singapore. “We see Singapore and the Middle East, in particular, as two very strong growth markets for us over the coming two to three years.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-03/barclays-to-more-than-double-singapore-private-bank-headcount>
Only 1,000 of 6,000 people who work for Apollo are investment professionals. The rest work for Athene and are busy selling annuities. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-04/how-leon-black-built-and-reinvented-apollo-money-to-burn-review?taid=6a9d9516db980e0001a4b9a6&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Citadel wants to buy US oil production assets from WildFire energy. (USNews) <https://money.usnews.com/investing/news/articles/2026-09-04/exclusive-hedge-fund-giant-citadel-seeking-to-buy-us-shale-oil-production-assets-sources-say>
Jefferies bonuses might not be so great this year. Now it seems that the bank has$500m worth of exposure to iron ore trader Radiant World and another entity. Once again, this makes it among the biggest creditors in a second high-profile alleged fraud. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/6bde3e74-9a7c-4528-9b9c-42a14eec0414?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Singapore-based hedge fund QuantEdge </news/quantedge> is up 40% this year. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/this-hedge-fund-gained-over-40-despite-ai-market-chaos-b0e7c457>
American white collar workers are quitting jobs at their lowest rate in years. When they move jobs they want big pay rises after salaries were held back in their current roles. But there's little hiring and many job advertisements are not what they seem. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-06/labor-day-2026-is-a-reminder-job-openings-are-scarce-for-american-workers?taid=6a9d78396f262700017baf82&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
A mysterious 2018 architecture graduate from Leeds Beckett University was paid £6,148,400 in the 2023-24 financial year. (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/money/family-finances/article/britains-highest-earning-graduate-was-making-6m-after-five-years-8tk6h2qv5>
27-year-old Griff Washburn lives an itinerant life on a sailing boat, hikes miles, cycles and kayaks. He also appears to make $300k a year on Spotify. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/music/goth-babe-artist-griff-washburn-b8d7550f?mod=rssfeed>
